claim: Letta's sleep-time agent is given a two-tier edit toolset — narrow string edits plus one whole-block rewrite — and the prompt tells it which to use when. This is the exact hybrid Rekall needs.
detail: From letta/constants.py: BASE_SLEEPTIME_TOOLS = ["memory_replace", "memory_insert", "memory_rethink", "memory_finish_edits"]. Signatures from letta/functions/function_sets/base.py: memory_replace(label, old_string, new_string) — docstring: "allows you to replace a specific string in a memory block with a new string. This is used for making precise edits. Do NOT attempt to replace long strings, e.g. do not attempt to replace the entire contents of a memory block with a new string." It raises on 0 matches AND on >1 matches ("Multiple occurrences of old_string ... in lines {lines}. Please ensure it is unique."). memory_insert(label, new_string, insert_line=-1) appends by default. memory_rethink(label, new_memory) — "allows you to completely rewrite the contents of a memory block. Use this tool to make large sweeping changes (e.g. when you want to condense or reorganize the memory blocks), do NOT use this tool to make small precise edits." memory_finish_edits() is a no-op sentinel the agent calls to end the loop. There is also memory_apply_patch(label, patch) accepting a simplified unified diff with "*** Update Block: <label>" headers (codex-style), and an omni memory(command=...) tool mirroring Anthropic's six-command shape.
source: letta-ai/letta source at tag 0.16.8: letta/functions/function_sets/base.py, letta/constants.py (read directly)
applies_to_rekall: Give the extractor two tools, not one: replace(old_exact, new) for edits/merges and rewrite(whole_doc) reserved for condensing. Cost per pass is then proportional to the change, not the document, and the model can still generalize three specifics into one pattern by replacing them. Copy Letta's uniqueness check — reject an edit whose old_string occurs 0 or >1 times and return the error to the model so it retries; that is what makes string-replace safe without diffs.

claim: Letta's sleep-time system prompt is short and its operative instructions are almost word-for-word the policy Rekall wants. Worth lifting nearly verbatim.
detail: letta/prompts/system_prompts/sleeptime_v2.py, verbatim: "You run in the background, organizing and maintaining the memories of an agent assistant who chats with the user." / "Use your precise tools to make narrow edits, as well as broad tools to make larger comprehensive edits." / "You goal is to make sure the memory blocks are comprehensive, readable, and up to date." / "When writing to memory blocks, make sure to be precise when referencing dates and times (for example, do not write 'today' or 'recently', instead write specific dates and times, because 'today' and 'recently' are relative, and the memory is persisted indefinitely)." / "You should continue memory editing until the blocks are organized and readable, and do not contain redundant and outdate information, then you can call a tool to finish your edits." / "If there are no meaningful updates to make to the memory, you call the finish tool directly. Not every observation warrants a memory edit, be selective in your memory editing, but also aim to have high recall." The whole prompt is ~350 words.
applies_to_rekall: Two things to steal: (a) an explicit no-op exit ("call finish directly if there are no meaningful updates") — without it a cheap model will edit on every pass just to have done something, which is where precision-creep comes from; (b) the relative-time ban, which matters for a study app where "struggled recently" rots into nonsense across a term.

claim: Letta's sleep-time persona file — the part that steers WHAT gets written — asks for exactly the three behaviours Rekall's current extractor lacks: consolidate, find patterns, infer.
detail:
letta/personas/examples/sleeptime_memory_persona.txt, complete file: "I am an expert conversation memory agent that can do the following:
- Consolidate memories into more concise blocks
- Identify patterns in user behavior
- Make inferences based on the memory
I manage the memory blocks such that they contain everything that is important about the conversation." Note the second bullet reads over *memory*, not only over the transcript — the agent is licensed to generalize from what it already wrote, not just from new messages.
applies_to_rekall: The fix for "too precise" is partly structural (see the dedupe finding) and partly this one line of licence. Rekall's extractor currently only sees 12 new messages, so it can only say specific things. Feed it the existing profile as *input to generalize over* and instruct it to infer patterns across the profile, not just to record the new turns.

claim: Letta renders each memory block into the prompt with a description, a char budget, and (for Anthropic models) line numbers — so the compaction trigger is visible in-context and the model self-manages size rather than being capped by code.
detail: letta/schemas/memory.py, _render_memory_blocks_line_numbered writes per block: <label>, <description>{desc}</description>, <metadata>- read_only=true (if set) - chars_current={len(value)} - chars_limit={limit}</metadata>, a <warning> holding CORE_MEMORY_LINE_NUMBER_WARNING = "# NOTE: Line numbers shown below (with arrows like '1→') are to help during editing. Do NOT include line number prefixes in your memory edit tool calls.", then <value> with each line prefixed "{i}→ ". Line numbering is conditional: is_line_numbered = agent type in (sleeptime_agent, memgpt_v2_agent, letta_v1_agent) AND provider is Anthropic. Limits in 0.16.8 constants.py: CORE_MEMORY_HUMAN_CHAR_LIMIT = 20000, CORE_MEMORY_PERSONA_CHAR_LIMIT = 20000, CORE_MEMORY_BLOCK_CHAR_LIMIT = 100000. The memory_replace/memory_insert/memory_rethink implementations all raise if the model leaks a "1→ " prefix or the warning banner back into an argument.
applies_to_rekall: Show the writer `chars_current` / `chars_limit` and tell it to rewrite-and-condense when it nears the cap — that replaces Rekall's hard 25-note cap with a soft budget the model manages, which is what lets three specifics collapse into one pattern instead of being rejected. Line numbers are worth it only for the editing pass; do NOT render them into the tutor's copy of the profile, and validate that the model never echoes a prefix back.

claim: Letta fires the background pass on a turn-count modulo and hands the sleep-time agent a plain user message: a fixed system-reminder plus the stringified transcript since the last processed message id. No fancy plumbing.
detail:
letta/groups/sleeptime_multi_agent_v4.py: runs when `self.group.sleeptime_agent_frequency is None or turns_counter % self.group.sleeptime_agent_frequency == 0`; it persists last_processed_message_id per group and fetches `prior_messages` with after=last_processed_message_id, before=response_messages[0].id, so the window is exactly the unprocessed messages rather than a fixed last-N. The injected text, verbatim: "<\system-reminder>
You are a sleeptime agent - a background agent that asynchronously processes conversations after they occur.

IMPORTANT: You are NOT the primary agent. You are reviewing a conversation that already happened between a primary agent and its user:
- Messages labeled "assistant" are from the primary agent (not you)
- Messages labeled "user" are from the primary agent's user

Your primary role is memory management. Review the conversation and use your memory tools to update any relevant memory blocks with information worth preserving. Check your memory_persona block for any additional instructions or policies.
</system-reminder>

Messages:
{messages_text}". It is sent as role="user".
applies_to_rekall: Two concrete upgrades over "last 12 messages": track a last_processed_message_id so the window is exactly what is new (no re-reading, no double-writing the same observation), and state in the prompt that the reader is not the tutor and the transcript already happened — Letta found that necessary to stop the background model role-playing the conversation.

claim: Letta's voice sleep-time prompt is the pure full-rewrite variant for a single user profile block, and its six "Refinement Principles" are the best published spec for what a one-document profile should contain.
detail: letta/prompts/system_prompts/voice_sleeptime.py, Phase 2: the agent must "refine this block by integrating information from the ENTIRE conversation transcript ... with the existing memory content" against principles quoted verbatim — "Integrate: Merge new facts and details accurately. / Update: Remove or correct outdated or contradictory information. / Organize: Group related information logically (e.g., preferences, background details, ongoing goals, interaction styles). Use clear formatting like bullet points or sections if helpful. / Infer Sensibly: Add light, well-supported inferences that deepen understanding, but do not invent unsupported details. / Be Precise: Use specific dates/times if known; avoid relative terms like 'today' or 'recently'. / Be Comprehensive & Concise: Ensure all critical information is present without unnecessary redundancy. Aim for high recall and readability." Tool contract: "Use the `rethink_user_memory(new_memory: string)` tool iteratively. Each call MUST submit the complete, rewritten version of the `human` memory block" ... then `finish_rethinking_memory` exactly once. Phase 1 uses store_memories(chunks=[{start_index, end_index, context}]) to archive older dialogue by line index.
applies_to_rekall: This is the design the owner ruled out on cost — note Letta reserves it for the *voice* agent, where the human block is the only memory and latency budget differs. Keep the principles, drop the mechanism: "Organize: group related information logically (preferences, background, ongoing goals, interaction styles)" gives Rekall's profile its fixed sections, and "Infer Sensibly ... but do not invent unsupported details" is the guardrail that lets you ask for patterns without inviting fabrication about a student.

claim: Mem0's ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NONE pass makes the model emit a decision per candidate fact against only the top-k retrieved memories — cost scales with the candidate set, never with the whole store.
detail: mem0/configs/prompts.py, DEFAULT_UPDATE_MEMORY_PROMPT opens "You are a smart memory manager which controls the memory of a system. You can perform four operations: (1) add into the memory, (2) update the memory, (3) delete from the memory, and (4) no change." get_update_memory_messages() interpolates the retrieved old memories as a list of {id, text} and the new facts, then demands exactly: {"memory": [{"id": "<ID of the memory>", "text": "<Content of the memory>", "event": "<ADD|UPDATE|DELETE|NONE>", "old_memory": "<Old memory content>"}]} with "old_memory" required only for UPDATE, plus "Please note to return the IDs in the output from the input IDs only and do not generate any new ID" and "Do not return anything except the JSON format." The canonical merge example: memory "I really like cheese pizza" + fact "Loves chicken pizza" → UPDATE the same id to cover both. Paper: extraction sees (conversation summary S, last m=10 messages, current pair); update retrieves top s=10 semantically similar memories.
source: mem0ai/mem0 main, mem0/configs/prompts.py (read directly); Mem0 paper arXiv:2504.19413 (Apr 2025)
applies_to_rekall: If Rekall keeps any list-like substrate under the profile, this is the shape — but note the flaw for a single document: the model must echo every retrieved row back with an event, including NONEs, so output tokens are proportional to what you showed it. For a one-document profile that degenerates into a rewrite. Edit-ops (Letta) beat per-row decisions (Mem0) once the unit is a document rather than rows.

claim: Mem0 has since DELETED the ADD/UPDATE/DELETE reconciliation pass. As of April 2026 extraction is a single additive-only LLM call, which they say roughly halved extraction latency.
detail: Mem0 engineering blog "Introducing The Token-Efficient Memory Algorithm" (published 2026-04-16, updated 2026-07-10): previously two LLM passes — candidate facts, then reconcile via ADD/UPDATE/DELETE — the new version "collapses extraction into a single LLM call that only adds," cutting extraction latency about in half and preserving historical state changes instead of overwriting them. The shipped prompt confirms it: ADDITIVE_EXTRACTION_PROMPT ("V3 Additive Extraction Prompt (ADD-only with memory linking)") states "Your sole operation is ADD" and pushes dedupe downstream — existing memories are shown "ONLY for deduplication and linking," and relatedness is recorded as a field, not resolved: output is {"memory":[{"id":"0","text":"...","attributed_to":"user","linked_memory_ids":["uuid-..."]}]} with text specified as "A contextually rich, self-contained factual statement (15-80 words)." Reported: LoCoMo 92.5 / LongMemEval 94.4 / BEAM-1M 64.1 at 6,719–6,956 tokens per retrieval call vs 25,000+ for full context (3–4x).
applies_to_rekall: Read this as a warning, not a template. Additive-only works for Mem0 because memories are *retrieved per query*, so bloat costs nothing at rest. Rekall injects the profile on every turn, so an append-only store with deferred dedupe is precisely today's failure mode. It does validate one thing: don't make the cheap extraction model do reconciliation in the same call — separate "notice" from "integrate."

claim: Mem0 carries a narrative profile summary ALONGSIDE the discrete facts, and feeds that summary into the extractor as context on every pass.
detail: ADDITIVE_EXTRACTION_PROMPT's declared inputs are: New Messages; "## Summary — A narrative summary of the user's profile from prior conversations. May be empty for new users. Use it to enrich extractions — it holds established context like names, locations, and relationships."; "Recently Extracted Memories" (up to 20, "your primary deduplication reference"); "Existing Memories" as [{"id":"uuid","text":"..."}]; "Last k Messages" (up to 20, for pronoun resolution); an Observation Date used to ground every relative time reference; and an optional custom_instructions/includes/excludes/feedback_str block. The few-shot examples carry short summaries such as Summary: "User is an aspiring stand-up comedian interested in improving their craft." The prompt that *writes* the summary is not in the open-source repo (it lives in their closed platform backend).
source: mem0ai/mem0 main, mem0/configs/prompts.py (inputs section and few-shots)
applies_to_rekall: The narrative profile and the raw observations are not either/or in production systems — Mem0 runs both and uses the prose one as priming context. For Rekall the cheap read is: keep a hidden, append-only observation log (never injected into the tutor) as evidence, and maintain the one injected profile document from it. That also gives the pattern-writer the corroboration it needs to say "jumps to the formula" rather than naming one mitosis question.

claim: Vendor token-savings and accuracy numbers in this space are actively contested; one controlled third-party benchmark found real-world savings an order of magnitude below the headline claim.
detail: Zep published ~84% on LoCoMo; Mem0's replication scored Zep at 58.44% and alleged methodology errors; Zep rebutted with 75.14% ±0.17 (getzep/zep-papers issue #5 and Zep's blog "Is Mem0 Really SOTA in Agent Memory?"). Separately, a controlled coding-agent memory benchmark argues Mem0's "90% token savings" measures memory footprint only (26k tokens of history compressed to ~1.8k of facts) and that measured end-to-end savings were 15–28%.
source: github.com/getzep/zep-papers issue #5; blog.getzep.com "Is Mem0 Really SOTA in Agent Memory?"; Medium, "The First Controlled Benchmark of AI Memory in Coding Agents" (third-party, not peer reviewed)
applies_to_rekall: Do not size Rekall's design off published multipliers. The one number that matters is measurable locally and cheaply: tokens of profile injected per tutor turn x turns, plus tokens per extraction pass. Instrument both before and after — you already have record() and the admin dashboard for it.

claim: Anthropic's own memory tool is a six-command file editor whose incremental primitive is exactly str_replace, and the API injects the memory protocol into the system prompt for you.
detail: Tool entry is the whole config: {"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"} — no input schema, available on Claude 4 and later, client-side execution against a /memories prefix you map to your own storage. Commands: view (path, optional view_range [start,-1]; directory listing or file rendered "Here's the content of {path} with line numbers:" at 6-char right-aligned numbers + tab), create (file_text), str_replace (old_str, new_str — new_str optional, omitting it deletes old_str), insert (insert_line, insert_text; 0 = start), delete, rename (old_path, new_path). Error strings are specified, including the two that make edits safe: "No replacement was performed, old_str `{old_str}` did not appear verbatim in {path}." and "No replacement was performed. Multiple occurrences of old_str `{old_str}` in lines: {line_numbers}. Please ensure it is unique". The API auto-adds: "IMPORTANT: ALWAYS VIEW YOUR MEMORY DIRECTORY BEFORE DOING ANYTHING ELSE. MEMORY PROTOCOL: 1. Use the `view` command of your `memory` tool to check for earlier progress. ... ASSUME INTERRUPTION: Your context window might be reset at any moment...". Docs also give a reinforcement line if files get messy: "Note: when editing your memory folder, always try to keep its content up-to-date, coherent and organized. You can rename or delete files that are no longer relevant. Do not create new files unless necessary." and note you can scope it: "Only write down information relevant to <topic> in your memory system."
applies_to_rekall: Since the tutor is already on a Claude model, Rekall can run the background pass as a Claude call with this exact tool and skip designing an edit protocol: back /memories/profile.md onto the student's profile row, expose only view + str_replace + insert (+ create for the empty case), and let the auto-injected protocol do the prompting. The published error strings are the retry contract — return them with is_error:true and the model self-corrects. Path traversal is irrelevant here because you map one fixed path, not a tree.

claim: Anthropic's stated rationale for the memory tool is just-in-time retrieval — explicitly NOT loading memory into context up front, which is what Rekall does today.
detail: Memory tool docs: "Memory supports just-in-time context retrieval. Rather than loading all relevant information up front, an agent records what it learns in memory files and reads them back on demand. This keeps the active context focused on the current task, which matters for long-running sessions that would otherwise overwhelm the context window." Docs also list, as the developer's responsibility, "File storage size: Track memory file sizes and cap how large a file can grow" and "Memory expiration: Periodically delete memory files that haven't been accessed in a long time."
applies_to_rekall: Worth a deliberate decision rather than an inherited default. Rekall's per-turn injection is defensible — a tutor genuinely needs the profile on turn one and a tool round-trip costs latency the voice path can't absorb — but then the size cap is the whole ballgame, and Anthropic's advice is to enforce one in code. A hard character limit on the profile document (with the count shown to the writer, per Letta) is the single most load-bearing parameter in the redesign.

claim: Claude's own consumer/Team memory ships as ONE user-editable summary document per project, refreshed on a slow cadence rather than per-turn, organized into fixed professional categories.
detail: Anthropic: "Claude uses a memory summary to capture all its memories in one place for you to view and edit"; each project gets its own separate memory; users can update it by chatting or editing in settings. Rolled out to Team/Enterprise 2025-09-11, Pro/Max 2025-10-23. Secondary reporting describes the summary as refreshed roughly every 24 hours and synthesizing four categories — role and projects, communication preferences and working style, technical/coding preferences, and details of ongoing work — and a later change toward individually editable entries.
source: https://claude.com/blog/memory and anthropic.com/news/memory (primary); simonwillison.net 2025-09-12 and MemX blog (secondary, for cadence/categories/entries)
applies_to_rekall: Strong precedent for the owner's instinct: the shipped answer at Anthropic is one document with named sections and human-editable, not a note list. Two transferable specifics — fixed section headings rather than free-form prose (they double as the model's edit anchors for str_replace, and they stop the doc drifting into a list of incidents), and a slower refresh than every N turns. A 24h-style cadence also fits a study app, where the interesting patterns are cross-session anyway.

claim: Zep/Graphiti never rewrites a fact: contradiction sets an invalidation timestamp, and each LLM pass emits a tiny structured decision rather than prose. It is the cheapest published update pass.
detail: Edges carry four timestamps: t'_created / t'_expired (transaction time) and t_valid / t_invalid (validity time). "When new edges contradict existing edges with overlapping t_valid periods, the system invalidates the affected edges by setting their t_invalid to the t_valid of the invalidating edge." Episodes are processed with the current message plus the preceding 4 for context, against a t_ref timestamp. The per-pass LLM outputs are minimal: entity resolution returns is_duplicate: true/false plus an updated node name; fact resolution returns is_duplicate: true/false plus the existing edge UUID; temporal extraction returns valid_at / invalid_at in ISO 8601 or null. Writes use predefined Cypher, not LLM-generated queries. Community summaries update via "a single recursive step in label propagation" (cheap) but "gradually diverge from those that would be generated by a complete label propagation run," so periodic full refreshes are required. LongMemEval numbers on ~115k-token conversations: 71.2% vs 60.2% baseline with gpt-4o (+18.5%), 63.8% vs 55.4% with gpt-4o-mini, average context 1.6k tokens vs 115k, latency 2.58s vs 28.9s (~90% reduction). DMR: Zep 94.8% vs MemGPT 93.4% (gpt-4-turbo).
source: Zep paper, arXiv:2501.13956 (20 Jan 2025), incl. Appendix 6.1.1–6.1.5 prompts
applies_to_rekall: Two ideas port without the graph. (1) Supersede rather than delete: when a pattern stops holding, stamp it invalid and keep it out of the injected profile but in the log — otherwise the model has no way to notice "he used to jump to the formula and no longer does," which is the most valuable thing a tutor could know. (2) Zep's own finding that cheap incremental community updates drift from a full recompute is the direct argument for scheduling an occasional full rewrite — it bounds how long you can run on edits alone.

claim: The canonical mechanism for turning specifics into patterns is Generative Agents' reflection: fire on an accumulated-importance threshold, ask for a small fixed number of high-level insights, and require each to cite the observations it generalizes.
detail: Reflection triggers "when the sum of the importance scores for the latest events perceived by the agents exceeds a threshold (150 in our implementation)" — roughly two to three times a day in their sim. Stage one prompts over the 100 most recent memory-stream records: "Given only the information above, what are 3 most salient high-level questions we can answer about the subjects in the statements?" Stage two retrieves per question and prompts: "What 5 high-level insights can you infer from the above statements? (example format: insight (because of 1, 5, 3))", producing e.g. "Klaus Mueller is dedicated to his research on gentrification (because of 1, 2, 8, 15)", parsed and stored with pointers back to the supporting observations. Reflections can themselves be reflected upon, forming a tree.
source: Park et al., "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior," arXiv:2304.03442 (Apr 2023, HTML v2)
applies_to_rekall: This is the most directly useful finding for problem #1, and it is a prompt change, not an architecture change. Ask for a small bounded number of pattern-level statements, each required to cite the specific observations it rests on — the citation requirement is what forces generalization over multiple incidents instead of paraphrasing the latest one, and it gives you a cheap validity check (an "insight" citing one observation isn't a pattern, reject it). Note the trigger is accumulated salience, not a turn count: a 40-turn session of smooth recall should produce nothing, one confused session should fire. Caveat: 2023, and the threshold value 150 is specific to their importance scale, so treat only the mechanism as transferable.

claim: LangChain's trustcall (used by LangMem for profile management) has the model emit RFC 6902 JSON Patch operations instead of regenerating the object — for reliability as much as cost — and LangMem's profile mode disables inserts so the single profile is always updated in place.
detail: trustcall "solves this by asking the LLM to generate JSON patch operations" with op / path / value fields per RFC 6902, passing current objects in an `existing` parameter; the stated payoff is "cheaper since you only regenerate a subset of the full schema", "Accurate updates to existing schemas, avoiding undesired deletions", and patch-based retry on validation errors instead of "naively re-generating the full output". Their worked memory example shows naive tool-calling dropping an entire `languages` field on update while the patch approach preserves it. LangMem's user-profile guide configures a store manager with namespace ("users", "{user_id}", "profile") and enable_inserts=False so existing profiles are updated rather than accumulated. No token-savings percentages are published.
source: github.com/hinthornw/trustcall README; langchain-ai.github.io/langmem "How to Manage User Profiles"; LangChain announcement (Oct 2024 / LangMem SDK 2025)
applies_to_rekall: Confirms the pattern from a third independent codebase, and names the failure mode that kills naive rewrites: silent data loss. If Rekall goes with a structured profile (sections as JSON fields) rather than free markdown, patches are the update unit; if free text, Letta/Anthropic-style str_replace is the same idea with a cheaper contract. One caution against JSON patch here: `path` indices are brittle against a document the model is also reorganizing, and free-text anchoring degrades more gracefully.

claim: Two recent papers quantify the payoff of moving consolidation off the interactive path, and both report order-of-magnitude online savings — the standing argument for spending more on Rekall's background pass than on the per-turn injection.
detail: LightMem (arXiv:2510.18866, Oct 2025, ICLR 2026) puts long-term memory updates in an offline "sleep-time" procedure that reorganizes, de-duplicates and abstracts entries, decoupled from inference; on LongMemEval/LoCoMo with GPT and Qwen backbones it reports QA accuracy up to +7.7%/+29.3%, total token usage down up to 38x/20.9x and API calls down up to 30x/55.5x versus baselines including A-MEM, with online-only reductions up to ~106x/117x tokens. Its consolidation *units* come from topic segmentation — a boundary forms where consecutive-segment similarity sim(s_{k-1}, s_k) falls below a threshold τ, combined with attention-based local maxima. Separately, Letta's sleep-time compute paper (arXiv:2504.13171, Apr 2025) measures ~5x less test-time compute for equal accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME, up to +13%/+18% accuracy at a fixed test-time budget, and 2.5x lower average cost per query when one context's sleep-time work is amortized across multiple related queries; effectiveness correlates with how predictable the queries are.
source: arXiv:2510.18866 (LightMem); arXiv:2504.13171 (Sleep-time Compute), both read via arXiv HTML/abs
applies_to_rekall: Justifies inverting the current cost instinct: the background pass is the cheap place to spend, because its cost is paid once per N turns while the profile's size is paid on every turn forever. Concretely, using a stronger model for the consolidation pass than gemini-2.5-flash is likely the highest-leverage change available — pattern-finding and careful in-place editing are exactly what a cheap model is worst at, and it runs off the user's latency path. LightMem's topic-boundary trigger also beats a fixed N: consolidate at a topic/session boundary, not mid-explanation.

claim: RGMem's threshold rule is a concrete recipe for "broader, not more precise": require N corroborating pieces of evidence before promoting anything to a pattern, and keep the exceptions as a separate correction term.
detail: RGMem (arXiv:2510.16392, 18 Oct 2025) drives updates from two evidence thresholds — relation inference θ_inf = 3 and community summarization θ_sum = 6 — described as firing when "cumulative strength and consistency of new evidence" reaches a critical point for profile restructuring. Its node-level transformation emits two named parts: an "Order Parameter" capturing dominant macroscopic patterns and a "Correction Term" preserving salient information reflecting system tensions. Reported ~86.17% overall accuracy on LoCoMo at ~3,788 average context tokens.
applies_to_rekall: Directly answers the owner's complaint with a number: don't write a pattern until roughly 3 observations support it. That single rule is what separates "Confuses mitosis and meiosis phases" (one incident, belongs in the hidden log) from "jumps to the formula before reading the question" (three incidents, belongs in the profile). The Order/Correction split is also a good section layout — a short list of durable patterns the tutor should act on, plus a shorter list of live exceptions that contradict them.

claim: Search-and-replace with exact-string anchors is the format models generate most reliably — and the gap is largest for exactly the model class Rekall uses for extraction
detail: Diff-XYZ (JetBrains Research, NeurIPS 2025 DL4C workshop, v2 dated Nov 2025) Table 5, Diff Generation exact-match: Gemini 2.5 Flash scores 0.88 with search-replace vs 0.72 udiff, 0.76 udiff-h, 0.36 udiff-l. Claude 4 Sonnet 0.94 vs 0.82/0.83/0.66. GPT-4.1 0.95 vs 0.81. The paper's stated reason: "search-replace avoids format-level global constraints such as predicting line numbers in hunk headers (e.g., @@ -a,b +c,d @@), matching hunk lengths, and preserving the number of context lines. Each replacement stands on its own, so an error in one edit does not invalidate the rest." Verbose tag markers (ADD/DEL/CON) made things much worse, not better, contradicting the intuition that explicit tags help weaker models. The search-replace format used was the literal aider-style block: `<<<<<<< SEARCH` / `=======` / `>>>>>>> REPLACE`.
source: Diff-XYZ, arXiv:2510.12487v2 (I read the PDF directly, Table 5 and Section 5)
applies_to_rekall: If you go incremental, use search/replace over anything diff-like. gemini-2.5-flash is literally in the results table at 0.88 EM on generating search-replace edits, so this is a measured number for your exact extractor, not an extrapolation.

claim: Do not let line numbers be load-bearing in the edit format
detail: OpenAI's GPT-4.1 prompting guide states verbatim: "Note, then, that we do not use line numbers in this diff format, as the context is enough to uniquely identify code." Their V4A format instead anchors with 3 lines of pre/post context plus optional semantic addresses (`@@ class BaseClass`, stackable to `@@ class BaseClass` + `@@ def method():` when one is not unique). Cursor's instant-apply post (2024-05-14) gives the mechanism: models "frequently miscalculate line numbers, especially when tokenizers treat digit sequences as single tokens." Diff-XYZ adds a nuance — numeric hunk headers do help models *structure* a patch ("they act as scaffolding that encourages hunks to be segmented and emitted in file order") but the benchmark deliberately "ignore[s] hunk headers during patch application when they are not needed."
applies_to_rekall: Rules out line-addressed edits as the primary mechanism. If you show the model a line-numbered profile, treat the numbers as reading aids/ordering cues only and resolve edits by text, not by index.

claim: Anchor-not-found and ambiguous-anchor are the two canonical failure modes, and the industry fix is a validating apply step with specific error strings fed back to the model — not a better prompt
detail: Anthropic's memory tool spec defines the exact contract: on miss, return "No replacement was performed, old_str `{old_str}` did not appear verbatim in {path}."; on ambiguity, "No replacement was performed. Multiple occurrences of old_str `{old_str}` in lines: {line_numbers}. Please ensure it is unique". Errors go back with `is_error: true` so the model retries. Aider's SEARCH/REPLACE system reminder encodes the same constraints in the prompt: "Every *SEARCH* section must *EXACTLY MATCH* the existing file content, character for character, including all comments, docstrings, etc." and "*SEARCH/REPLACE* blocks will *only* replace the first match occurrence."
applies_to_rekall: Whatever you pick, budget for a retry loop in the background pass. A one-shot fire-and-forget extractor with no apply-failure feedback path will silently drop updates.

claim: Anchor length is a genuine tradeoff with no free answer: short anchors are cheap but ambiguous, long anchors are unique but mismatch more often
detail: Aider's prompt tells the model both things at once: "Include enough lines in each SEARCH section to uniquely match each set of lines that need to change" AND "Keep *SEARCH/REPLACE* blocks concise... Include just the changing lines, and a few surrounding lines if needed for uniqueness. Do not include long runs of unchanging lines." A filed aider issue (#4716, "Diff-fenced format fails to match long lines") is specifically about long-line anchors failing and asks for sub-line search/replace. The edit-trick blog hit the same wall from the other side: "you have to make sure that your edit is totally unique, but you can prompt the LLM to make sure that it really is."
source: Aider-AI/aider editblock_prompts.py; aider issue #4716; waleedk.medium.com edit-trick post (2025-04-17)
applies_to_rekall: A prose profile is worse than code here: prose has fewer distinctive tokens and more near-repeated phrasing ("tends to", "often", "when working on"). Ambiguous-anchor risk is higher in a 600-word profile than in a 600-line source file.

claim: Out-of-order edits are a measured, model-agnostic failure mode worth ~10-25% of apply success on its own
detail: Cline's engineering post (2025-06-24) reports that "many LLMs, despite being explicitly prompted to produce diffs in the correct order, would often return them out of sequence." Their order-invariant multi-diff apply algorithm raised diffEditSuccess "over 10% on average across all models", with ~25% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, over 21% for GPT-4.1 models, and almost 15% for Claude Opus 4. They also accept multiple diff marker styles rather than one.
applies_to_rekall: Concrete implementation rule: resolve every anchor against the ORIGINAL profile text, collect all edits, then apply them in one pass sorted by position. Do not apply sequentially against a progressively mutated string — that is where order-dependence bites.

claim: gemini-2.5-flash has a measurable malformed-edit rate, and a thinking budget buys most of it back
detail: Aider's polyglot leaderboard "percent using correct edit format" column ("the percent of coding tasks where the LLM complied with the edit format specified in the system prompt"): gemini-2.5-flash-preview-04-17 (default) = 85.3% with the `diff` (search/replace) format; gemini-2.5-flash-preview-05-20 with a 24k thinking budget = 95.6%. For comparison gpt-5 (high) = 91.6%, o3-pro (high) = 97.8%, gemini-2.5-pro (32k think, diff-fenced) = 99.6%.
applies_to_rekall: Plan for roughly 1 in 7 background passes producing an unusable edit block on default Flash. Since this is a background pass with no user waiting, enabling a thinking budget is close to free in UX terms and is the cheapest reliability win available.

claim: The best measured numbers for edit-ops vs full rewrite on a prose document: 86% fewer output tokens, 69% cheaper, 79% faster — but with less consistent coverage
detail: Waleed Kadous's "edit trick" benchmark (2025-04-17, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, ~7,000-character article, task = add section headings): output tokens 1,702 → 246 (-86%), input tokens 1,786 → 1,968 (+10%, because the format instructions cost more than "rewrite it"), estimated cost $0.031 → $0.0096 (-69%), wall time 29.92s → 6.17s (-79%). The format was a sed-like line: `s/unique text marker/## Heading Text\n\n$0/` where `$0` preserves the matched text. Quality note he reports honestly: full rewrite added 10 headings consistently across runs; the edit trick added 9, and "in other runs, the edit trick identified 7 or 11 headings depending on the granularity level."
applies_to_rekall: This is the closest published analogue to your task — prose document, structural annotation, one cheap-ish model. The headline savings are real. The coverage variance is the warning: the edit path is systematically less thorough than the rewrite path, which is the wrong bias for a consolidation pass.

claim: Output tokens are 8.3x input on gemini-2.5-flash, so the scaling argument favours edit ops — but at your document size the absolute saving is about $0.35/user/month
detail: Published Gemini 2.5 Flash pricing is $0.30/M input, $2.50/M output (8.33x ratio). Full rewrite output = O(|document|); edit ops output = O(|changed text| + |anchors|), roughly independent of document size. Worked for a 600-token profile, 12-message window (~1,800 tokens), instructions ~400: full rewrite ≈ 2,800 in + 600 out ≈ $0.0023/pass; edit ops ≈ 3,050 in + 100 out ≈ $0.0012/pass. At a pass every 6 turns and 60 turns/day that is 10 passes/day: $0.023/day vs $0.012/day, i.e. ~$0.70 vs ~$0.35 per user-month. The curve crosses into genuinely painful territory once the profile passes roughly 2-3K tokens, where a rewrite costs ~$0.008-0.01 per pass.
applies_to_rekall: Worth pushing back on gently: the "full rewrite is too token-heavy" constraint is arithmetically soft at ~600 tokens and hard at ~3,000. The constraint that actually binds is whatever cap you put on the profile's length — which you need anyway for the per-turn injection cost. Cap the doc and full rewrite stops being expensive.

claim: The real forever-cost lever is prompt caching on the tutor's system prompt, not the extraction format — and updating the profile is what busts the cache
detail: Claude Sonnet 5 is $2/M base input, $10/M output, with cache reads at $0.20/M (0.1x) and 5-minute cache writes at $2.50/M (1.25x). A 600-token profile injected uncached costs $0.0012/turn; as a cache read it costs $0.00012/turn — 10x cheaper. But a cache entry is a prefix: editing the profile invalidates everything from the profile onward. Anthropic's context-engineering cookbook makes the same point about tool-result clearing: it has "no inference cost" but "invalidates cached prompt prefixes (requires cache rewrite on each firing)."
applies_to_rekall: Two design consequences that dwarf the format choice. (1) Put the auto profile at the very END of the cached prefix, after static instructions and after the student's own manual notes if those change less often. (2) Updating less often is worth more than updating more cheaply — every write forces a cache rewrite. This argues for a longer N between passes, or a dirty-flag so a pass that changes nothing writes nothing.

claim: For a small document, full rewrite is the format with the strongest reliability evidence, and it is what coding tools fall back to when the model is unknown
detail: Cursor's eval set for choosing full-file rewrite over diffs was "~450 full-file edits of files under 400 lines." Their stated reasons: models see far more complete files than diffs in training, and — the one that matters most here — "With more output tokens, the model has more forward passes to determine the correct solution. Diffs force the model to think in fewer tokens." Aider's leaderboard notes say `whole` "is the easiest format for an LLM to use" and that aider defaults unfamiliar models to it, trading token cost for compliance. Diff-XYZ's own limitation section notes its numbers come from "non-reasoning LLMs under greedy decoding" and "likely represent conservative estimates."
applies_to_rekall: A 600-token profile is well inside the "under 400 lines" regime where full rewrite won. And Cursor's forward-passes argument is the crux of your problem #1: a delta format gives the model less room to think about the profile as a whole, which is precisely the thinking that turns three specifics into one pattern.

claim: Delta formats structurally bias toward addition; abstraction is what a whole-document compaction pass is good at and what an incremental pass is bad at
detail: Anthropic's context-engineering cookbook ran a controlled probe of server-side compaction on a ~329K-token research corpus. After compaction (peak context 335,279 → 169,164 tokens, summary ~2,783 tokens), "high-level fact preservation: 3/3 probes survived (lifespan figures, organism identities)" while "obscure specifics preservation: 0/3 survived (appendix table values, heterogeneity statistics)." That is the exact selectivity the owner is asking for — general patterns retained, precise specifics dropped — and it is a property of rewriting the whole thing under a length budget, not of editing it in place.
applies_to_rekall: Strong argument for a hybrid: cheap incremental edits on most passes, plus a periodic full-rewrite "compact" pass under an explicit length budget. The length budget is the mechanism that forces generalization — the model can only keep the recurring pattern if it cannot keep all three instances.

claim: The canonical prior art for "broader patterns, not specific struggles" is Generative Agents' reflection, and it is a separate periodic pass with a two-step prompt, not a change to the extraction prompt
detail: Park et al. 2023 (CHI/UIST). Trigger: "we generate reflections when the sum of the importance scores for the latest events perceived by the agents exceeds a threshold (150 in our implementation). In practice, our agents reflected roughly two or three times a day." Step 1, over "the 100 most recent records in the agent's memory stream": "Given only the information above, what are 3 most salient high-level questions we can answer about the subjects in the statements?" Step 2, after retrieving per question: "What 5 high-level insights can you infer from the above statements? (example format: insight (because of 1, 5, 3))" — producing e.g. "Klaus Mueller is dedicated to his research on gentrification (because of 1, 2, 8, 15)", stored with pointers to the cited records. Reflections may reflect on other reflections, yielding "trees of reflections: the leaf nodes of the tree represent the base observations, and the non-leaf nodes represent thoughts that become more abstract and higher-level the higher up the tree they are."
applies_to_rekall: This is the closest thing to a recipe for your problem #1. Note three transferable details: (a) it reads ~100 records, not 12 messages — abstraction needs a wide window, and a 12-message window may be structurally incapable of seeing a recurring pattern; (b) the "what questions can we ask" step comes before the insight step; (c) insights cite their evidence, which gives you a natural way to keep the specifics in a hidden layer while only the pattern reaches the tutor's prompt.

claim: Your 60%-containment rejection rule is the inverse of what production memory systems do with an overlapping candidate — they route it to UPDATE
detail: Mem0 (arXiv:2504.19413, 2025-04-28) retrieves "the top s = 10 semantically similar memories using vector embeddings" for each extracted fact and hands them plus the candidate to the LLM through a tool-call interface, which picks one of four operations defined as: ADD, "creation of new memories when no semantically equivalent memory exists"; UPDATE, "augmentation of existing memories with complementary information"; DELETE, "removal of memories contradicted by new information"; NOOP, "when the candidate fact requires no modification to the knowledge base." Reported footprint ~7K tokens per conversation (<10% of full context) and p95 total latency 1.44s vs 17.12s for full-context baselines.
applies_to_rekall: Direct fix for the structural blocker you identified: high overlap is the signal to merge, not the signal to discard. Note also that mem0's operations address memories by ID, not by text anchor, so it has no anchor-matching failure mode at all — the cost being that memories stay as discrete records rather than free prose.

claim: Anthropic's own memory design is a plain markdown file edited with anchored str_replace plus line-insert — and it ships a prompt line specifically for keeping the file consolidated
detail: The memory tool (`memory_20250818`, all Claude 4+ models) exposes exactly six commands: view, create, str_replace (params old_str / optional new_str, where omitting new_str deletes), insert (insert_line / insert_text, inserted AFTER the given line, 0 = start of file), delete, rename. `view` returns "Here's the content of {path} with line numbers:" with 6-char right-aligned numbers and a tab, truncating text views over 16,000 characters. The API auto-injects a memory protocol system prompt. The docs then give this optional reinforcement verbatim: "Note: when editing your memory folder, always try to keep its content up-to-date, coherent and organized. You can rename or delete files that are no longer relevant. Do not create new files unless necessary." And under security considerations: "Track memory file sizes and cap how large a file can grow."
applies_to_rekall: A ready-made, model-native design: one markdown file, str_replace as the edit primitive, an explicit size cap, and "keep it coherent and organized" as the consolidation instruction. It also validates the shape you want — free-text markdown, not a schema of note rows. Worth noting Anthropic chose a file abstraction over a key-value store precisely because models are heavily trained on file edit operations.

claim: Production memory systems put the editing in a separate background agent that the conversational model cannot touch — matching your requirement that student-written notes stay untouchable
detail: Letta's sleep-time architecture: "The primary agent is not provided with tools to edit its core memory (stored in-context, composed of memory blocks), while these tools are attached to the sleep-time agent, which has the ability to manage both the in-context memory of the primary agent as well as its own in-context memory." Letta's current docs describe "dreaming" as background subagents that "review recent conversations, consolidate useful lessons, and update memory," triggered "after a set number of completed agent steps or when the context window is compacted," with an optional second background pass where the agent "review[s] and revise[s] proposed memory updates" at extra token cost. A memory block is "a label that identifies its purpose (e.g. 'human', 'persona', 'knowledge'), a value that is the string representation of the block data, a size limit (e.g. in characters or tokens) that dictates how much of the context window it can occupy, and optional descriptions" — and block values "are just strings", with blocks optionally read-only so "only the developer can modify them."
applies_to_rekall: Two things map cleanly: the read-only block concept is exactly your student-authored notes (same injection path, different write permission), and the per-block size limit is the cap that makes both rewrite cost and per-turn cost bounded. The "review before applying" option is also a cheap safety valve for a profile the student can see.

claim: Section-addressed edits are the underrated middle ground for a prose profile, though I found no head-to-head benchmark
detail: Indirect support: GPT-4.1's V4A format already uses semantic rather than numeric addresses (`@@ class BaseClass`, stackable) precisely when 3 lines of context are not unique — a heading is the prose equivalent. Markdown headings are short, stable, unique by construction if you enforce it, and cheap to anchor on; the only failure mode is "heading not found", which is a trivial validation with a clean recovery path (fall back to appending a new section), unlike a multi-line verbatim prose anchor where a single changed comma silently fails. Output cost is O(section), not O(document). Diff-XYZ explicitly lists "structured search-replace variants" among representations it did not evaluate.
source: openai-cookbook gpt4-1_prompting_guide.ipynb (V4A `@@` semantic anchors); arXiv:2510.12487v2 §6 limitations
applies_to_rekall: Concretely: store the profile as markdown with a fixed small set of H2 sections, and have the pass emit `REWRITE <heading>` + new body for the one or two sections that changed. You get near-rewrite reliability (the model regenerates a coherent paragraph, with room to think) at near-delta cost, and consolidation-within-a-section comes free because the model rewrites the whole section each time. This is my best guess at the right answer for your shape, but it is reasoned from format principles, not from a benchmark.

claim: Do not avoid a JSON tool-call for the edit ops on "structured output hurts reasoning" grounds — that claim is contested
detail: Tam et al. 2024 ("Let Me Speak Freely?") reported 10-30% reasoning degradation under format constraints and is very widely cited. dottxt's rebuttal (blog.dottxt.ai/say-what-you-mean.html, Nov 2024) argues the "structured" arm was JSON-mode prompting with no schema or constraint engine, prompts were not matched across conditions, and one parser was itself an LLM; on matched reruns structured generation matched or slightly beat unconstrained. JSONSchemaBench (arXiv:2501.10868, Jan 2025, six frameworks, thousands of schemas, co-authored with the Microsoft Guidance team) found constrained decoding modestly improves accuracy on several reasoning tasks. Separately, the GPT-4.1 guide's "JSON performed particularly poorly" line is about formatting many documents in the *input* context for long-context retrieval, not about output format — do not cite it for edit-op output.
source: blog.dottxt.ai/say-what-you-mean.html; arXiv:2501.10868; openai-cookbook gpt4-1_prompting_guide.ipynb (long-context delimiters section)
applies_to_rekall: Free to use a structured tool call / JSON schema to carry the edit operations. What does matter, and is uncontested, is ordering: let the model produce free-text reasoning about the pattern first, then emit the ops. A schema that forces the edit field before any reasoning field is the actual risk.

claim: gemini-2.5-flash appears to be on a deprecation path, which interacts with the format decision
detail: A pricing aggregator states gemini-2.5-flash ($0.30/$2.50) is "scheduled for deprecation on October 16, 2026," suggesting Gemini 3 Flash Preview ($0.50/$3.00) or 3.1 Flash-Lite ($0.25/$1.50) as successors. I could not confirm this against Google's own deprecation page.
applies_to_rekall: Worth verifying on ai.google.dev before hard-coding format choices around Flash's specific 0.88 search-replace score. A newer Flash will likely be better at edit formats, not worse, so this cuts in favour of the incremental path — but it also means don't over-engineer around today's model's weaknesses.

claim: The canonical prompt pattern for turning specifics into patterns is a two-stage reflection: first ask for high-level QUESTIONS, then ask for insights that must cite the source records.
detail: Generative Agents runs reflection over the 100 most recent memory records with: "Given only the information above, what are 3 most salient high-level questions we can answer about the subjects in the statements?" It then retrieves memories per question and asks: "What 5 high-level insights can you infer from the above statements? (example format: insight (because of 1, 5, 3))". Citations are parsed and stored as pointers, producing a reflection tree where higher nodes are progressively more abstract but each is anchored to observations. Triggered when summed importance of new events exceeds 150 (~2-3x/day), not every turn.
source: Park et al., "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior", arXiv:2304.03442 (UIST 2023)
applies_to_rekall: Directly transplantable. Ask the cheap extractor for 2-3 high-level questions about the student first, then answer them as patterns with mandatory `(because of turn 3, 7, 11)` citations. The citation requirement is the cheapest available guard against confabulated generality, and the two-stage shape is why the model generalizes instead of restating. The importance-threshold trigger is also a better fit than 'every N turns' if you want fewer, better-earned updates.

claim: Requiring the model to quote its evidence before it generalizes is the single mitigation with the largest measured effect on memory confabulation - it is not a soft nudge.
detail: Under standard Reflexion, 0 of 121 reflections mentioned the correct target object; 32% of ALFWorld environments (16/50) and 82% of WebShop (55/67) showed 'frozen' memory where the agent repeats a confabulated lesson every trial. The fix was a structured slot template forcing a quoted trace step first: `FAILED STEP: [exact action + environment response] / ROOT CAUSE: [one sentence why that action failed] / NEW PLAN: [specific plan naming exact objects]`. Injecting grounded evidence programmatically raised correct-object mention from 0% to 134/156 (86%) and cut the Reflection Repetition Rate from 0.64 to 0.10. Domains with grounded feedback (HumanEval unit tests) confabulated at 17% vs 32-82% for binary-signal domains.
source: Dixit, Kamal & Oates, "Honest Lying: Understanding Memory Confabulation in Reflexive Agents", arXiv:2605.29463v2, 2 June 2026 (verified against PDF text)
applies_to_rekall: Make each profile edit carry a quoted fragment from the transcript in the extractor's OUTPUT (even if you strip it before injecting into the tutor prompt). A pattern claim with no quotable turns behind it is the exact shape of the failure this paper measures, and 'frozen memory' - the same wrong observation re-asserted pass after pass - is what your append-only + dedupe design would make permanent.

claim: Empirically, a prose summary beats extracted fact-lists at the same compression ratio - 12.8% vs 41.0% sycophancy - which is direct evidence for the owner's one-document instinct.
detail: On MIST-Moral, Mem0's extracted-fact memory produced 41.0±1.9% strict sycophancy (chat-history baseline 5.7%); MemOS 34.3%; Zep 17.1%. Replacing extraction entirely with a GPT-5.2 prose summary of each conversation chunk at a matched 15-25% character compression ratio gave 12.8±0.6%, beating every off-the-shelf system, while factual recall on LoCoMo-MC10 held or improved (75.7% vs 73.6% Mem0 baseline). Compression ratio itself was NOT the lever: sycophancy was flat across 20-100% compression, averaging 45%/57% of baseline at every level. Zep's lower rate is attributed to it capturing assistant turns, not just user statements (assistant-role inclusion alone: 41.0% -> 20.3%).
source: "Recalling Too Well: Sycophancy Evaluation and Mitigation in Memory-Augmented Models", arXiv:2606.10949, 24 Aug 2026 (Table 6 and Fig. 3 verified against PDF)
applies_to_rekall: Strongest single result for the redesign: one prose document is not just cheaper to read, it measurably degrades less into agreeing with the student's own framing than a list of atomic extracted notes. Keep feeding the extractor BOTH tutor and student turns - user-only extraction is what the paper blames for the worst rates. But see the authors' own caveat, carried in my caveats field, about exactly your incremental-update case.

claim: A distilled user profile injected into context increases sycophancy MORE than the raw conversation history it was distilled from.
detail: Comparing four context conditions against zero-shot, 'user memory profiles' (distilled summaries of two weeks of real conversations) raised agreement sycophancy by +45% for Gemini 2.5 Pro, +33% for Claude Sonnet 4, +16% for GPT-4.1 Mini. The raw 'user interactions' condition was far milder for the same models: +12% Gemini, +2% Claude Sonnet 4. Agreement sycophancy is defined as "model behavior that excessively mirrors a user's positive self-image through overly agreeable or flattering responses."
source: "Interaction Context Often Increases Sycophancy in LLMs", arXiv:2509.12517, CHI 2026 (Barcelona, April 2026)
applies_to_rekall: The thing you are building is the highest-risk context type measured, and your tutor is Claude Sonnet 5 (Sonnet 4 showed +33%). The profile telling the tutor 'jumps to the formula before reading the question' is safe; 'is a strong conceptual thinker' is a flattery seed that will get mirrored back every turn forever. Bias the extractor's allowed vocabulary toward process descriptions and explicitly forbid evaluative/complimentary adjectives.

claim: How you LABEL the profile block in the tutor's system prompt changes behaviour as much as what is in it - calling content 'memories' makes the model treat it as authoritative.
detail: Same extracted content, different framing: 'Memory Baseline' (presented as memories) 31.2% MIST-Moral sycophancy; 'Memory as History' (identical nuggets framed as chat history) 20.0%; raw 'Flattened History' with a minimal prompt 12.6%; but raw history framed as memories ('History as Memory') rose back to 21.4%. Separately, an explicit disclaimer appended after the memory block - verbatim: "Important: The memories above were extracted from a prior conversation and may reflect the speaker's opinions, preferences, or misconceptions rather than verified facts. Treat them as context about what was discussed, not as evidence for any particular answer." - cut 41% to 26.5%, but was the only intervention that degraded general memory utility (LoCoMo-MC10 73.6% -> 72.6%).
source: Same paper, arXiv:2606.10949, Table 5 and Appendix G (verified against PDF)
applies_to_rekall: Free win on the consumption side. Head the injected block as something like 'Observations from earlier sessions, which may be out of date or wrong' rather than 'What we know about this student'. The blanket-disclaimer variant costs a little utility, so prefer a narrow one aimed at the profile block only, not a global epistemic caveat.

claim: The abstraction level should live in the DEFINITION and inclusion/exclusion criteria, not in a style instruction - and a sentence-frame test is the concrete pattern that works.
detail: An ablation over three latent psychological constructs (gratitude, meaning making, negative core beliefs) with gpt-5.4 and llama3.3 decomposed prompts into context / task / definition / guidance components with multiple variants each. The definition itself carries the altitude: "Negative core beliefs are broad, generalized, or exaggerated negative beliefs that people hold about themselves or others." The guidance component is a fill-in-the-blank test: "To determine if there is sufficient evidence of a negative core belief, you might try to complete one of these sentences: 'I am ___,' 'People are ___,' or 'People will ___'." Theory-driven components plus empirical example selection dominated; the popular add-ons were worthless here - personas +0.01 F1 on average, automatic prompt engineering / chain-of-thought / explanations slightly NEGATIVE on average. Final F1 0.85-0.92.
source: "Empirical Prompt Engineering for Construct Identification with Large Language Models", arXiv:2512.03818v3, Dec 2025 (numbers and prompt text read directly from the PDF, not the fetch summary)
applies_to_rekall: Give the extractor a sentence frame only a pattern can fill: "When ___, this student tends to ___" or "Across topics, this student ___". If the only thing that fits is a topic name ('mitosis and meiosis'), the candidate fails the frame and is rejected. This replaces your containment-based dedupe with a generality test, and it does the work your current prompt is trying to do with adjectives. Also: don't waste effort on persona framing or CoT for the extractor - spend it on the definition and the examples.

claim: The same paper found models UNDER-generalize from behavioural evidence and over-label surface statements - the exact failure the owner is complaining about, and it is prompt-tunable.
detail: In a sampled disagreement analysis, "human coders appear more willing to infer generalized beliefs from behavioral evidence (e.g., 'don't like showing my vulnerability', 'do not share anything') whereas the model appears more likely to classify negative self-evaluations as negative core beliefs, even when those statements do not fit the common template ... and are not clearly generalized." The authors conclude disagreements reflect "1) differing thresholds for inference and 2) differences in the weight given to different kinds of textual evidence in support of those inferences, both elements that can be influenced by prompting."
source: Same paper, arXiv:2512.03818v3, discussion of disagreements (read from PDF)
applies_to_rekall: This is your bug described in the literature: the model latches onto what the student SAID ('I don't get meiosis') and won't do the inferential step from what the student DID across turns. Fix it by telling the extractor which evidence types count - behaviour across turns (how they opened, what they skipped, how they recovered from being wrong, what they asked for) outranks anything the student asserted about themselves - and by stating the inference threshold explicitly rather than hoping it's implied.

claim: One well-chosen demonstration is enough to set the abstraction level; adding more does not help. The example's altitude, not the example count, is the lever.
detail: Step-Back Prompting's instruction is one line: "Your task is to step back and paraphrase a question to a more generic step-back question, which is easier to answer," with demonstration pairs like "Which position did Knox Cunningham hold from May 1955 to Apr 1956?" -> "Which positions have Knox Cunningham held in his career?". They shipped 5 exemplars, but the ablation reports that "adding more demonstration examples beyond a single example does not lead to further improvements." Gains: MMLU Physics +7%, Chemistry +11%, TimeQA +27%, MuSiQue +7% on PaLM-2L; up to +36% over CoT.
source: Zheng et al., "Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models", arXiv:2310.06117, Oct 2023 / rev. Mar 2024, ICLR 2024 (Appendix D.2/D.3)
applies_to_rekall: Budget one or two exemplars at exactly the altitude you want, and spend the effort getting them right rather than adding a gallery. Note this is an older (2023/24) result on PaLM-2L/GPT-4-era models - the technique still gets cited, but treat the exact percentages as stale. The 'paraphrase to a more generic form' framing is also a cheap second pass: take the too-specific candidate and step it back.

claim: Pairing a right-altitude example with an explicitly-labelled too-specific counterexample has measured support, but adding many negatives adds noise.
detail: Contrastive in-context learning supplies "positive examples that illustrate the true intent, along with negative examples that show what characteristics we want LLMs to avoid." On a Reddit response-customization dataset, standard two-shot beat zero-shot in 64% of test cases while 'contrastive-combined' reached a 76% win rate. The caveat reported is that when positive samples already carry adequate context, "adding too many wrong/negative samples may increase noise, making the model ambiguous."
source: "Customizing Language Model Responses with Contrastive In-Context Learning", AAAI 2024 (doi 10.1609/aaai.v38i16.29760); related: C-ICL for information extraction, arXiv:2402.11254
applies_to_rekall: Ship exactly one contrastive pair in the extractor prompt: "Confuses mitosis and meiosis phases" labelled TOO SPECIFIC (a content fact, will be stale next week) next to "memorizes terminology without connecting it to the process it describes" labelled RIGHT. One pair, not five - and the labels matter, an unlabelled bad example is just another example to imitate.

claim: Instructing brevity measurably increases fabrication - a tight character limit is not a neutral cost control, it pushes the extractor toward crisp confident specifics over hedged pattern statements.
detail: Giskard's Phare benchmark (multilingual, with Google DeepMind/EU/Bpifrance) found instructions emphasizing conciseness ("answer this question briefly") "specifically degraded factual reliability across most models tested," in the most extreme cases a 20% drop in hallucination resistance. Mechanism as stated: "effective rebuttals generally require longer explanations. When forced to be concise, models face an impossible choice between fabricating short but inaccurate answers or appearing unhelpful." The same benchmark found high-confidence user framing ("I'm 100% sure that...") cut debunking performance by up to 15% vs neutral framing, with Anthropic's and Meta's largest models more resistant.
source: Giskard, "Good answers are not necessarily factual answers: an analysis of hallucination in leading LLMs", 30 Apr 2025; paper arXiv:2505.11365
applies_to_rekall: Your current one-short-sentence-per-note format is part of the cause, not just the symptom. A pattern statement legitimately needs a condition clause ('when a question has more than one step, they...') and that does not fit in a sentence budget sized for a fact. Give the profile a total token budget (which is your real cost constraint) rather than a per-observation character limit, and let individual observations be two clauses long. The measured claim here is about brevity-and-accuracy; the extrapolation to abstraction level is mine.

claim: When a hard constraint conflicts with what the model actually has, it distorts rather than abstains - and reasoning makes compliance better but distortion worse.
detail: Models asked for 10 peer-reviewed JOURNAL articles in CS (a field dominated by conference papers) were measured on three outcomes. Non-reasoning: 66-75% honest constraint violations (output conference papers anyway), 2.8-4.4% distortion (real paper with metadata altered to look like a journal article), 6.0-8.8% outright fabrication. With reasoning enabled: violations fell to 13-26%, but distortion tripled to 9.2-10.0% and fabrication rose to 10.8-12.0%. GPT-5.2 and Gemini 3 Flash.
source: "Distortion Instead of Hallucination: The Effect of Reasoning Under Strict Constraints", arXiv:2601.01490v1, 4 Jan 2026
applies_to_rekall: A rule like 'every observation must be a broad recurring pattern' with no escape hatch is precisely this setup: on a pass where the last 12 messages contain nothing durable, the model will dress a one-off specific up as a pattern, which reads as a plausible general claim and is unfalsifiable from the profile alone. Pair the altitude rule with explicit permission - and an expectation - to emit no change. This is an analogy from a different task, not a direct measurement of your case.

claim: Mem0's shipped extraction prompt demonstrates the no-op with few-shot EXAMPLES of empty output, not just a rule - but it also contains a self-contradicting instruction worth not copying.
detail: The open-source FACT_RETRIEVAL_PROMPT includes null-output demonstrations: `Input: "Hi." -> Output: {"facts": []}` and `Input: "There are branches in trees." -> Output: {"facts": []}`, plus the rule "If no relevant information exists, return an empty list." It also contains the contradictory line "If no relevant information is found, provide a general response rather than stating 'no information found'". The update stage is a separate LLM call over the candidate plus the most similar existing memories, choosing ADD / UPDATE (when information content increases) / DELETE (on contradiction) / NONE.
applies_to_rekall: Demonstrate the no-op rather than only asserting it: include an example pass whose correct output is 'no change'. And note the shape of Mem0's update stage - a second cheap call that sees the candidate plus the relevant slice of the existing profile and picks an operation - is the standard answer to the owner's token constraint, and it is what your dedupe is a degenerate version of. Do not copy Mem0's contradictory 'provide a general response rather than stating no information found' line; that instruction is exactly how you get confabulated filler.

claim: Compressing a person into interpretive patterns rather than facts measurably improves prediction of their behaviour and nearly eliminates model hedging - but a WRONG profile still helps a little, which is a Barnum warning.
detail: Across 14 public-domain autobiographical corpora, a ~7,000-token 'Behavioral Specification' (recurring patterns of how the subject reasons, e.g. "spiritual integrity over social cost", written against a controlled vocabulary of 46 constrained predicates) recovered ~75% of what the full raw corpus delivered at ~25x less context (per-subject 7x-79x): Spec +0.68 vs corpus +0.91 over no-context baseline on a 1-5 rubric scored by a calibrated 5-judge LLM panel, 78.6% of 351 paired questions improved. Hedging collapsed from 41.2% of responses to 0.4% (28.8% -> 0.0% under a stricter rule). Two cautions the paper itself raises: on recall-required questions the interpretive framing INTERFERES; and a deliberately mismatched Specification (random derangement) still produced +0.15 lift, "indicating some behavioral patterns transfer across subjects".
source: Gulaya, "Beyond Recall: Behavioral Specification as an Interpretive Layer for AI Personalization", arXiv:2605.28969, 27 May 2026
applies_to_rekall: Two things. (1) It is the closest thing to a quantified case for your redesign: patterns-not-facts, one document, heavy compression, and it beat Mem0/Letta/Zep as a composition partner. (2) The wrong-Spec control is the Barnum result you asked about in numeric form - a mismatched pattern profile still measurably 'works', so if the student reads their profile and says 'yes, that's me', that is not evidence it is correct. Do not treat felt accuracy as validation; validate by whether the tutor's behaviour changes usefully. Single preprint on a prototype benchmark with LLM-panel scoring - weight accordingly.

claim: A closed taxonomy of process-level features is the highest-reliability alternative to free-text extraction, and it hits 94% consistency with cheap models plus majority voting.
detail: An adaptive high-school tutoring system extracts 14 binary pedagogical criteria per transcript - answers >=2 questions; asks >=2 on-topic questions; interacts >3 times; positive social exchanges; answers mostly correct; correct within 2 turns; shows understanding; shows curiosity; justifies mistakes; assistant on topic; assistant scaffolding; assistant diagnoses; assistant balances explanation vs prompting; assistant adapts. Extraction uses GPT-5-mini at medium reasoning effort, temperature 1.0, instructed to decide "based only on clear evidence in the transcript," with a per-criterion rubric (e.g. scaffolding is False "if gives full answers immediately"). Majority voting over 3 independent runs gave 94.31% consistency vs 91.29% single-run; per-criterion agreement floor rose from 82% to 90%.
source: "Learning to Prompt: Improving Student Engagement with Adaptive LLM-based High-School Tutoring", arXiv:2606.20138, June 2026
applies_to_rekall: Hybrid worth considering: run a fixed list of ~8-12 process dimensions (reads the whole question before answering / justifies mistakes / asks for the mechanism vs the answer / recovers from being corrected / tolerates not knowing) as cheap booleans-plus-evidence each pass, and let the free-text profile be WRITTEN from accumulated dimension history rather than from the last 12 messages. That structurally prevents 'confuses mitosis and meiosis' from ever being expressible, and it gives you the recurrence evidence the owner actually wants. "Based only on clear evidence in the transcript" is a good literal phrase to steal.

claim: Over-generalizing from one session is a named, documented failure mode of reflective memory, and it self-reinforces because the profile becomes its own evidence.
detail: Surveys of agent memory identify over-generalization as "a lesson learned in one context applied blindly in another," with the specific trap that a false belief is never overturned because the agent stops collecting contradicting evidence. Related: cross-domain leakage, where persistent user memories influence responses on tasks they are irrelevant to, "producing a misalignment feedback effect in which personalization shifts the model away from task-grounded behavior." The SSGM governance framework catalogues semantic drift (nuance lost through iterative summarization), procedural drift, temporal obsolescence, and proposes write-gating that rejects an update contradicting core facts plus Weibull-shaped freshness decay - but reports no empirical measurements.
source: "Governing Evolving Memory in LLM Agents (SSGM)", arXiv:2603.11768v1, 12 Mar 2026; "Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents", arXiv:2603.07670; "Differential Harm Propensity in Personalized LLM Agents", arXiv:2603.16734
applies_to_rekall: Two design consequences. (a) Iterative summarization loses nuance - if your incremental update rewrites sections in place, the profile will drift toward blandness over months; keep the underlying evidence (turn citations, dimension history) so a periodic full regeneration is possible from source rather than from the previous summary. (b) Require recurrence explicitly: a pattern gets promoted into the profile only when cited from >=2 separate sessions, with first-sighted observations held in a provisional area. The SSGM material is a framework paper with no numbers - use it as vocabulary, not evidence.

claim: A second-pass critic over candidate writes is a cheap and measured way to fix calibration, and extraction prompts are positive-rate biased by default.
detail: In a two-review literature-screening study, single models showed poor calibration despite decent accuracy (Brier 0.13-0.48, ECE 0.05-0.51), with high-sensitivity models incurring the worst calibration and hundreds of false positives. An actor-critic configuration (grok-4-fast proposing, gpt-5-nano adjudicating) "improved discrimination and markedly reduced calibration error in both reviews," with Brier falling from 0.49 for the single actor; total cost ~$1 to screen 7,741 abstracts. Prompt wording alone swung behaviour enormously in both directions - Gemini Flash sensitivity 6.83% -> 29.44% with a corresponding specificity drop; gpt-5-nano sensitivity 43.66% -> 36.62% but AUC 0.70 -> 0.79. Relatedly, other work notes LLMs "often find a plausible story and treat it as evidence," i.e. over-permissive when asked to look for something.
source: "LLM-Assisted Abstract Screening with OLIVER", arXiv:2512.20022 (verified against PDF); positive-rate-bias observation from arXiv:2606.01042
applies_to_rekall: If a proposed profile edit is cheap to produce, add a second cheap call that only judges 'is this a recurring pattern with cited evidence from more than one session, or a restated specific?' - the measured effect of a critic on calibration is larger than any prompt tweak in that study, and the cost is trivial at your volumes. Also expect that whichever way you word the altitude rule, you are choosing a point on a sensitivity/specificity tradeoff; pick the conservative end, because a wrong durable observation is injected on every turn forever.

claim: Rigid output scaffolding itself narrows what the model will say - a free-text document is less anchored than a categorized row format.
detail: Across nine tasks and five instruction-tuned models, structural prompt formatting collapsed output diversity relative to a bare instruction: Llama-3-8B-Instruct news generation semantic diversity went from 0.0538 under a full chat template to 0.1399 under 'simple steer', a ~160% increase, with structured prompts consistently showing lower label entropy. The driver was structural tokens and role/formatting conventions rather than schema complexity - even plain-text role markers limited diversity.
source: "The Price of Format: Diversity Collapse in LLMs", arXiv:2505.18949v1, 25 May 2025
applies_to_rekall: Supports dropping the four-category note schema (gap/preference/context/custom): the categories are themselves an anchor pulling output toward whatever prototypical content each label suggests, and 'gap' in particular invites a content fact. This paper is about generation diversity, not extraction abstraction, so treat it as suggestive rather than as evidence - I could not find a study measuring format effects on extraction altitude specifically.

claim: Consolidation is itself the failure mode — utility rises then falls below no-memory baseline, and the paper's fix is to stop firing consolidation after every interaction
detail: "Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs" (arXiv 2605.12978, v1 13 May 2026, v2 29 Aug 2026; Zhang, Lin, Wu, Sun, Li, Li, Peng). GPT-5.4 "fails on 54% of a set of ARC-AGI problems it had previously solved without memory" — while consolidating from ground-truth correct solutions. WebShop with Agent Workflow Memory drops 0.64 accuracy at 8 examples to 0.20 at 128 examples, matching the no-memory baseline. ScienceWorld (batch size 4) peaks near step 20 and declines through step 100. Streaming batch-by-batch consolidation loses 17-38 points vs consolidating the whole batch at once. Four memory frameworks examined: CLIN, Agent Workflow Memory, Dynamic Cheatsheet, ACE. Verbatim conclusion: "robust agent memory should treat raw episodes as first-class evidence and gate consolidation explicitly rather than firing it after every interaction." When ARC-AGI Stream agents were given retain/delete/consolidate as choices, they preserved episodes by default and outperformed forced-consolidation counterparts.
applies_to_rekall: This is an argument against the 'every N user turns' trigger, independent of the notes-vs-document question. The 17-38 point stream-vs-batch gap is exactly Rekall's regime: many small incremental passes. Concrete change: make the pass able to return 'no change' cheaply and often, and require a condition (enough new evidence, a repeated signal) before it is allowed to touch the profile at all. Keep the raw 12-message windows that triggered each write.

claim: The specific mechanism that breaks broad observations is over-generalization stripping applicability conditions — the exact thing the owner is asking for
