detail: Same paper isolates three pathologies: (1) misclassification during abstraction — dissimilar episodes grouped before summarizing, merging task families that should stay distinct; (2) over-generalization — "Abstraction can strip the applicability conditions of a lesson, so that overgeneralized entries interfere with neighboring tasks"; (3) overfitting to narrow streams — with limited input variety the consolidation fits instances rather than principles. Their framing of the cure: "Correct Segmentation Takes Time, Forced Abstraction Breaks It."
applies_to_rekall: "Jumps to the formula before reading the question" with no scope attached will fire on decks where it is fine, and the tutor will nag. Make the profile's pattern lines carry a when-clause and an evidence count — 'on multi-step physics problems (seen 4x, last 2026-09-14), jumps to the formula before reading the question'. That is the applicability condition the paper says abstraction silently deletes. Also: overfitting-to-narrow-streams means a student with 3 sessions on one deck will get a fake 'pattern'; gate on evidence breadth, not just count.

claim: There is a measured penalty for exactly the swap being proposed: incrementally rewriting one structured document loses 10.0pp vs an append-only flat fact list, and the recovery is a two-phase design, not a one-phase one
detail: "User as Code: Executable Memory for Personalized Agents" (arXiv 2606.16707, 16 Jun 2026, Bojie Li). Table 9 ablation on the first 5-conversation LOCOMO subset (300 QAs) with Gemini 3 Flash: Basic 3-tier 56.7% -> flat append-only facts 75.7% ("Adding append-only fact extraction ... gains +19.0pp on LOCOMO") -> incremental rewrite of a structured representation 65.7% ("Switching from flat facts to incremental code ... loses 10.0pp"), because "each session's code rewrite drops earlier facts" -> two-phase architecture 78.0%, "+12.3pp over Incremental code and +2.3pp over Flat facts," described as combining append-only preservation with typed structure. Repo: github.com/19PINE-AI/user-as-code.
applies_to_rekall: The most directly load-bearing number found. It says a profile-document-maintained-by-patches, on its own, is worse than the append-only note list Rekall already has; and that the winning configuration keeps the append-only layer and derives the structured view from it. Design implication: keep an append-only raw observation log (cheap, never rewritten, never injected) plus the prose profile as a derived, periodically-rebuilt view. Do not let the profile be the only copy.

claim: Coarse synthesized profiles beat atomic facts specifically on inference-heavy questions, but the winning systems keep all three granularities simultaneously
detail: TriMem, "Rethinking How to Remember: Beyond Atomic Facts in Lifelong LLM Agent Memory" (arXiv 2605.19952, May 2026). Three coexisting representations: raw dialogue segments anchored by source identifiers; extracted atomic facts as typed tuples (restatement, time, person, location...); and synthesized entity profiles aggregating scattered facts. LoCoMo with GPT-4o: TriMem 42.73 BLEU / 50.23 F1 vs Mem0 28.74/37.74, LightMem 36.26/47.37, SimpleMem 34.64/41.36. PerLTQA with Qwen3-8B: 92.46% profile / 83.23% social / 85.72% events vs SimpleMem 88.12/82.40/79.87. Their analysis: single-evidence questions rely on explicit factual content, but multi-evidence questions demand "emotional inference and logical induction" that only profiles capturing "personality traits, career background, interests, interpersonal dynamics and behavioral tendencies" support.
applies_to_rekall: Vindicates the owner's instinct — a synthesized prose profile is the right representation for the kind of judgement a tutor makes (pacing, framing, when to push). But the evidence is for profile-in-addition-to-facts, not profile-instead-of-facts. Same conclusion as the User-as-Code ablation from an unrelated team.

claim: MemoryOS makes 'recurring vs one-off' a counter, not a model judgement: a heat score gates promotion into the long-term user profile
detail: MemoryOS (arXiv 2506.06326, EMNLP 2025 main). Heat = alpha*N_visit + beta*L_interaction + gamma*R_recency with alpha=beta=gamma=1; N_visit is retrieval count, L_interaction is dialogue pages in the segment, R_recency = exp(-dt/mu) with mu = 1e7. Segments exceeding threshold tau = 5 are promoted from mid-term to long-term persona memory, where an LLM extracts and updates trait dimensions. Mid-term capacity 200 segments, eviction by lowest heat (not LRU). User KB and Assistant Traits are fixed-size 100-entry FIFO queues, so new facts displace the oldest. Reported average +49.11% F1 and +46.18% BLEU-1 over baselines on GPT-4o-mini.
applies_to_rekall: A cheap, non-LLM answer to the precision problem. Let the extractor keep writing precise observations into a staging log, and only let something into the injected profile when it has been observed N times across M sessions. The generalization then falls out of repetition rather than the model being asked to be wise. Note the FIFO-100 detail as a warning: their bloat bound silently drops the oldest facts, which is catastrophic forgetting by policy.

claim: The canonical published prompt for turning specifics into patterns is Generative Agents' reflection, and it is explicitly gated and cites its evidence
detail: Park et al., "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior" (arXiv 2304.03442 / UIST 2023). Reflection fires when the sum of importance scores of recently perceived events exceeds a threshold — 150 in their implementation, which in practice meant roughly two or three reflections per simulated day. The prompt takes the 100 most recent memory records and asks: "Given only the information above, what are 3 most salient high-level questions we can answer about the subjects in the statements?" The model then answers those questions, and each resulting insight is stored with pointers to the memory records that produced it. Retrieval scores each memory on recency (exponential decay since last access), importance (LLM rating), and relevance (cosine similarity).
applies_to_rekall: Two transferable pieces. (1) The prompt shape: ask for high-level questions the observations can answer, then answer them — this reliably produces pattern-level output where 'write a broad observation' produces vagueness. (2) Insights point back at their source records. A prose profile with no back-pointers loses this; keeping '(from 4 observations, most recent 2026-09-14)' inline preserves it at almost no token cost. Note the 2023 date — the prompt shape is durable, the retrieval scoring has been superseded.

claim: A dedupe rule that rejects overlapping writes is a named, benchmarked failure mode — MemFail calls it storage failure
detail: MemFail (arXiv 2605.26667v1, 27 May 2026; Garg, Kolhe, Song, Zhao — Berkeley). Four-mode taxonomy: summary failure ("'I am deathly allergic to peanuts' may be compressed into 'allergic to peanuts', stripping the severity critical for downstream reasoning"), storage failure ("the storage step does not adequately incorporate H' into M. This includes refusing to overwrite outdated facts (e.g., not updating 'Dan likes pizza' after the user states Dan now hates pizza)"), retrieval failure (returns "memories that are semantically similar but contextually inappropriate"), and reasoning failure. Five datasets across four tasks: Conditional-Facts, Coexisting-Facts, Persona-Retrieval, Long-Hop. Systems evaluated: Mem0, A-MEM, SimpleMem, StructMem. Finding on model strength: "stronger models do not improve accuracy while sometimes degrading accuracy on most tasks; smarter reasoning models can generate overly verbose memories that pollute the agent's context." Architecture matters more than model: "StructMem performs strongly on most tasks but fails spectacularly on Coexisting-Facts, while Mem0 shows the opposite pattern." Grading validated at 98% correct on 100 manually-graded examples.
applies_to_rekall: The 60%-containment reject rule is literally MemFail's storage failure: it blocks both the generalization (looks like a duplicate) and the correction (looks like a duplicate). Removing it is right. Separately, the finding that stronger models write more verbose, context-polluting memories is a defence of keeping gemini-2.5-flash as the extractor — do not assume upgrading the extractor model fixes the precision problem; it may make it worse.

claim: Zep/Graphiti handles staleness by invalidating rather than deleting, and rewrites the stale fact into past tense so it stays readable
detail: Zep engineering blog "Beyond Static Knowledge Graphs" (2 Oct 2024) plus the Zep paper. Every fact edge carries four timestamps: created_at and expired_at (when the system learned / stopped believing it) and valid_at and invalid_at (when it was true in the world). Invalidation is LLM-decided, not rule-based: "We make an LLM call for each new edge using an invalidation prompt, providing existing similar edges as context." On conflict the system sorts by valid_at and invalidates the edge that occurred earlier in the real world. Nothing is deleted — expired_at is set, and the fact text is regenerated into the past: "Maria works as a junior manager" becomes "Maria used to work as a junior manager, until her promotion to a senior manager." This supports point-in-time queries ("what was the user's plan in January?").
applies_to_rekall: Directly portable to a prose profile without a graph. When a pattern stops holding, do not delete the line and do not leave it asserted — move it to a short 'no longer holds' tail section, past-tensed, and stop injecting it. That preserves recoverability, gives the student something intelligible to read ('you used to skip the question stem; that stopped around September'), and is a pedagogically valuable artifact in a study app. Caveat: the blog is Oct 2024, so the implementation has likely moved on even if the model has not.

claim: Use-based exponential decay (Ebbinghaus) is the standard published staleness mechanism, and it strengthens on corroboration rather than just aging out
detail: MemoryBank (arXiv 2305.10250, AAAI 2024, SiliconFriend). Retention R = e^(-t/S), where t is time since the memory was last used and resets to 0 on each use, and S is memory strength, initialized to 1 and incremented every time the memory is used. Memories below a retention threshold are forgotten. SSGM (arXiv 2603.11768, Mar 2026) proposes a Weibull variant as a read-time filter: w(dt) = exp(-(dt/eta)^kappa), applied as a freshness threshold theta_fresh on retrieval rather than as a deletion policy.
applies_to_rekall: Gives a one-line staleness rule that needs no extra model calls: each profile line carries last_corroborated and a corroboration count; the injected profile includes only lines above a freshness bar. A pattern the student grew out of fades from the prompt on its own, and the fade is reversible because the line is still on disk. Confidence is medium because MemoryBank is a 2023 design and the specific coefficients are not validated for this use; the shape is well-established, the numbers are not.

claim: Bounding drift requires periodically reconciling against an immutable log, not against the previous profile — this is the one published claim with a formal bound
detail: SSGM (arXiv 2603.11768v1, 12 Mar 2026). Catalogues semantic drift ("iterative summarization causes gradual nuance loss"), procedural drift, goal drift, memory hallucination, temporal obsolescence, index bloat, memory poisoning, privacy leakage. Four mechanisms: pre-consolidation validation via a truth-maintenance contradiction check before a write lands; temporal and provenance grounding at read time; access-scoped retrieval; and reversible reconciliation via dual-track storage — a mutable active graph plus an immutable episodic log. Theorem 1 (Bounded Semantic Drift): naive systems accumulate O(T * eps_step) drift over T timesteps; with reconciliation every N steps, drift is O(N * eps_step), independent of the total horizon. Gated write (Eq. 6) rejects updates contradicting core facts.
applies_to_rekall: The practical recipe: most passes patch the profile incrementally (cheap, satisfies the token constraint), but every Nth pass rebuilds the profile from raw stored turns instead of from its own previous output. That caps drift at N passes' worth instead of letting it compound forever, and it is the only place a full rewrite is paid for. Confidence is medium because the paper is a framework proposal with no empirical results — the theorem is under assumptions, not a measurement.

claim: The self-confirmation trap is the named failure for a model reading its own prior inference, and the published fix is decoupling the writer from the reader
detail: EDV, "Escaping the Self-Confirmation Trap: An Execute-Distill-Verify Paradigm for Agentic Experience Learning" (arXiv 2606.24428, 23 Jun 2026). Verbatim: "existing experience learning methods mostly rely on single-agent loops, where the same agent executes tasks, summarizes outcomes, and determines memory content. This setup makes agents vulnerable to the Self-Confirmation Trap: wrong-but-self-consistent trajectories are misidentified as successful experience, leading to cumulative errors during retrieval and reuse." Fix: Execute (multiple heterogeneous agents in parallel), Distill (a dedicated third-party agent comparatively analyzes trajectories, "reducing executor-centric summarization bias"), Verify (the execution group validates candidates by consensus; "only approved experiences are written"). Evaluated on tau2-bench, Mind2Web, MMTB.
applies_to_rekall: Rekall already has half of this for free: gemini-2.5-flash writes the profile, claude-sonnet-5 reads it. Keeping the extractor a different model from the tutor is not just a cost decision, it is the documented mitigation — worth writing down so nobody 'simplifies' it later by having Sonnet maintain its own profile. The missing half is the verify gate. The cheapest version of verify in a consumer app is the student (see Cursor), not a second model.

claim: Memory sycophancy — the system absorbing user-stated falsehoods as durable fact — is now a benchmarked failure
detail: MemSyco-Bench (arXiv 2607.01071, v2 3 Jul 2026, XMU DeepLIT). Multi-turn conversations in which the user introduces factually incorrect statements; the system is later asked to recall, and the measure is whether it retains the original fact or adopts the user's false claim. Covers both RAG and pure memory architectures. Repo github.com/XMUDeepLIT/MemSyco-Bench, leaderboard at xmudeeplit.github.io/MemSyco-Bench-Leaderboard/.
applies_to_rekall: Relevant because a study tutor's profile is written largely from the student's self-report, and students are unreliable narrators about their own weaknesses ('I'm just bad at maths'). A self-assessment absorbed as a durable profile line will shape every future turn. Practical guard: record self-reports as claims with a speaker attribution ('says she is bad at fractions') rather than as findings ('is bad at fractions'), and let the tutor's own observed evidence be what promotes a claim to a pattern. Confidence low — I could not extract the measured rates.

claim: Anthropic's own memory tool gives you the exact incremental-edit primitive for a single document, including a built-in guard against blind clobbering
detail: Memory tool, type memory_20250818, name memory (platform.claude.com docs, read in full). Six commands: view (optional view_range [start, -1]), create (file_text), str_replace (old_str, optional new_str — omitting new_str deletes), insert (insert_line, insert_text; 0 inserts at the top), delete, rename. view returns line numbers 6 characters wide, right-aligned, tab-separated, 1-indexed, and truncates text views over 16,000 characters. str_replace failure strings: "No replacement was performed, old_str `{old_str}` did not appear verbatim in {path}." and, on ambiguity, "No replacement was performed. Multiple occurrences of old_str `{old_str}` in lines: {line_numbers}. Please ensure it is unique". The API auto-injects: "IMPORTANT: ALWAYS VIEW YOUR MEMORY DIRECTORY BEFORE DOING ANYTHING ELSE. ... ASSUME INTERRUPTION: Your context window might be reset at any moment...". Suggested reinforcement prompt if files get cluttered: "Note: when editing your memory folder, always try to keep its content up-to-date, coherent and organized. You can rename or delete files that are no longer relevant. Do not create new files unless necessary." Security section says outright: "Track memory file sizes and cap how large a file can grow" and "Periodically delete memory files that haven't been accessed in a long time."
applies_to_rekall: The token-efficient update mechanism the owner is asking for, already specified. Send the profile once with line numbers, have the extractor emit str_replace / insert ops rather than a full rewrite; cost is proportional to the change, not the document. Two free properties: the verbatim-match requirement means a failed edit errors instead of silently mangling the profile, and the uniqueness requirement stops one edit from hitting the wrong line. Third, and most useful for this design: an op list IS the diff, so 'show the student what changed' comes for nothing. The pattern is model-agnostic — you can implement the same op vocabulary against gemini-flash with a plain JSON schema.

claim: Letta bounds profile bloat with a hard character cap surfaced to the model as a tool error, and protects human-authored content with a read_only flag
detail: Letta memory blocks (docs.letta.com/guides/agents/memory-blocks/ read directly, plus letta-ai/letta issue #957). A block has label, description, value, limit, read_only (default false). Editing tools: memory_replace (find-and-replace), memory_insert, memory_rethink (full rewrite), memory_finish_edits; the deprecated pair was core_memory_replace / core_memory_append. Memory.compile() renders blocks as XML for most providers but uses a line-numbered format for Anthropic models. Exceeding limit throws an error the agent sees, which forces it to consolidate rather than silently truncating. Docs warn: "Setting value completely replaces the entire block content—it is not an append operation," and concurrent modification is "last write wins," risking data loss. read_only exists to prevent "potentially destructive changes" and is recommended for shared/organizational blocks. Third-party course material and issue threads give the default limit as 2,000 characters; Letta's own page did not state a default.
applies_to_rekall: Two off-the-shelf shapes. (1) Bloat bound: give the auto profile a character budget and return the overflow as an error to the extractor, so the model is forced to compress or drop something rather than the system silently dropping the tail — this makes the 25-note cap's successor fail loudly instead of quietly. (2) The student's own notes become a read_only block: the extractor can read them as context but the tool refuses writes, which is a stronger guarantee than instructing it not to touch them. Medium confidence only on the 2,000-char default, which I could not confirm from Letta's docs.

claim: Mem0's four-op vocabulary with NOOP as a first-class outcome, plus its measured token cost and an audit table with before/after values
detail: Mem0 (arXiv 2504.19413, Apr 2025). Extraction phase takes a message pair (m_{t-1}, m_t) plus a conversation summary and recent context; update phase retrieves the top s = 10 semantically similar memories and lets the LLM pick one of ADD (no semantic equivalent exists), UPDATE (complementary information), DELETE (contradicted), NOOP (repeat or irrelevant) via tool-calling rather than a separate classifier. Measured: 7k tokens per conversation for Mem0 vs 26k for full conversation history vs 14k for the graph variant vs 600k+ for Zep's graph. p95 latency 1.44s vs 17.12s for full-context (92% reduction, ~90% token saving), at 67.13 LLM-as-judge vs full-context's 72.90 — a 5.9-point accuracy cost. The history API returns id, memory_id, user_id, old_memory ("the previous state of the memory, if applicable"), new_memory, event in {ADD, UPDATE, DELETE}, created_at, updated_at, input messages, categories, session_id.
applies_to_rekall: Three things. (1) Make NOOP explicit and expected — the dominant outcome of a healthy pass is 'nothing durable happened', and naming it in the schema is what stops the model manufacturing an observation every time it is asked. (2) The 5.9-point gap vs full context is the honest price of any memory summarization; worth knowing before attributing tutor quality regressions to the new profile format. (3) old_memory/new_memory/event/created_at is the minimum viable undo table — one row per patch gives you rollback and a human-readable changelog without versioning the whole document.

claim: Anthropic's own consumer product moved in the opposite direction — from one rolling memory summary to individually editable categorized entries — and the stated reason is user control
detail: claude.com/blog/memory (11 Sep 2025) launched memory as a "memory summary" that captures "all its memories in one place for you to view and edit," updatable "at any time by chatting with Claude," scoped per project as a safety guardrail. The current help centre (support.claude.com article 11817273) now says: "Claude saves memory as a set of individual topics as you chat, rather than summarizing conversations after they end," with "Everything Claude remembers is listed under Topics" and per-topic read / edit / delete. Secondary reporting dates the switch to 10 July 2026 and gives the rationale as being able to change or delete one entry "without wiping everything Claude knows about you." Sensitive categories (health, race, ethnicity, religion, politics, gender identity) are excluded by default; IDs, criminal history, financial accounts and immigration status are never saved even on request.
applies_to_rekall: The strongest counter-signal to 'one big document'. A team that shipped the single-summary design replaced it with entries, and the reason was recoverability and granular user control — not model quality. The reconciliation for Rekall: the document is the right thing to inject into the tutor's prompt; entries are the right thing to show the student. Store patch-level records (or per-line provenance) so the student-facing view can be entry-granular even though the injected artifact is prose. Confidence medium: the entries-not-summaries state is primary-sourced, the July 2026 date and the rationale are secondary.

claim: Cursor converts model inference into confirmed fact with an explicit human approval step before a memory is saved
detail: Cursor memories are "automatically generated rules based on your conversations in Chat," project-scoped. A sidecar model observes the chat and proposes candidate memories — durable facts, repeated corrections, stated preferences, explained conventions — and "Cursor asks for your approval before a background-generated memory is saved"; background-generated memories wait for sign-off. Saved memories are listed and deletable under Settings → Rules & Memories. The stated principle in the community/docs framing: "an unreviewed memory is an invisible system prompt you never agreed to." Rules (author-written) and memories (extracted) are kept as distinct surfaces.
applies_to_rekall: The cheapest mechanism for the inference-vs-confirmed distinction, and it fits a tutor unusually well: the tutor can surface a candidate pattern conversationally ('I've noticed you tend to reach for the formula before finishing the question — does that sound right?'), and the answer promotes it from inference to confirmed. That also gives the student agency over their own profile, which is a product feature, not just a safety rail. Note Cursor's rules-vs-memories split mirrors Rekall's student-notes-vs-auto-profile split — the separation is validated by two independent products.

claim: A prose profile has no schema, so provenance has to be carried inline — and the failure when it isn't is that a generated conclusion becomes indistinguishable from an observation
detail: No single authoritative primary source; the pattern recurs across engineering writeups and issue trackers from 2026. Recurring field set per memory record: source_type (user statement / agent inference / tool output / third-party content), confidence at write time, created_at, last_accessed_at, source session id, and a human-readable provenance string distinguishing "User stated this explicitly" from "Inferred from behavioral patterns." The sharpest framing found: when categories collapse into one undifferentiated pool called "memory," "a generated conclusion becomes indistinguishable from an observation — the memory system has effectively laundered an inference into a premise." SSGM's read-time "temporal and provenance grounding" is the closest thing to a formal version. One extraction-prompt practice reported: "Only patterns with medium or high confidence are included, with output kept minimal."
source: Multiple 2026 engineering posts and GitHub design issues (metatech.dev, DigitumDei/agentpalace #157, Limes-Labs #600); SSGM arXiv 2603.11768
applies_to_rekall: Direct consequence of moving to free text: the current schema carries the category column, and a prose document throws it away. Replace it with inline markers the tutor can read and the student can audit — e.g. lines suffixed '[inferred, 4 sessions, last 2026-09-14]' vs '[student said, 2026-08-02]' vs '[confirmed with student, 2026-09-03]'. The tutor prompt should then instruct different behaviour per marker: act on confirmed, probe inferred, never assert inferred back to the student as fact. Low confidence on the field list being canonical — it is a widely-repeated convention, not a published standard.

claim: LongMemEval quantifies how badly deployed memory systems handle knowledge updates and temporal reasoning — the staleness categories are the worst ones
detail: LongMemEval (arXiv 2410.10813, ICLR 2025) evaluates five abilities: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention. Commercial assistants and long-context LLMs show roughly a 30% accuracy drop on retaining information across sustained interactions; on a simplified version of the benchmark ChatGPT dropped 37% and Coze 64% relative to reading the context directly. LongMemEval_S is ~115,000 tokens over ~40 sessions per user; _M extends to ~500 sessions. Recent per-category results put temporal reasoning at 59.4% and multi-session recall at 52.6%.
source: arXiv 2410.10813; secondary summaries for per-category numbers
applies_to_rekall: Calibrates expectations: the 'observation was true in March, false in June' case is the hardest category in the literature, and shipped consumer systems lose 37-64% on it. Do not expect the extractor to notice a pattern has stopped holding. Design for it structurally — decay so uncorroborated lines fade, and a periodic rebuild-from-raw so a stale line cannot survive indefinitely just because it is already written down.

claim: Codex's memory docs explicitly warn against treating hand-editing as the control surface — a tension Rekall inherits the moment students can edit the auto profile
detail: learn.chatgpt.com customization/memories doc: "Codex can turn useful context from eligible prior chats into local memory files"; it "updates memories in the background instead of immediately at the end of every chat"; "Memories may not update right away when a chat ends." Files live at ~/.codex/memories/ and users are told to "review memory files before sharing your Codex home directory" — but also, verbatim: "don't rely on editing them by hand as your primary control surface."
applies_to_rekall: If the student edits a line in the auto profile and the next incremental pass overwrites it, the edit is silently lost and trust in the feature dies. Two workable resolutions: (a) a student edit pins the line — the extractor sees it marked as pinned and its ops against it are rejected; or (b) a student edit promotes the line out of the auto profile into their own notes, where the extractor cannot reach it at all. Option (b) reuses the separation the owner already committed to.

claim: ChatGPT bounds memory with a soft word budget plus eviction, and surfaces every write inline at the moment it happens
detail: Two independently switchable pools: "saved memories" (extracted or explicitly asked for) and "reference chat history." Updates are surfaced in-conversation as a "Memory updated" indicator that expands to "Manage memories," from which every entry can be read or forgotten; users can also ask in chat what it remembers and tell it to forget things. Multiple secondary sources give the bound as a soft limit of roughly 1,500 words / ~200 memories, after which older memories are compressed or dropped, and report a 'memory is full' state that blocks new writes until entries are deleted. Memories are excluded from model training.
source: openai.com memory announcement and help centre (both returned HTTP 403 to fetch); figures from descript.com, aimemory.pro and other secondary summaries
applies_to_rekall: The inline 'Memory updated' affordance is the cheapest transparency win available and costs no tokens: when a pass writes, show a small chip in the tutor thread that opens the diff. That single UI element covers most of the recoverability requirement. The ~1,500-word figure is worth noting only as a rough order of magnitude for what a consumer-scale profile budget looks like — I could not verify it from OpenAI directly, so do not quote it as a target.

claim: OpenAI publicly replaced the discrete saved-memories list with a synthesized free-text "memory summary" as the user-facing artifact — the exact move Rekall is making — and shipped it on 2026-06-04.
detail: Primary source: openai.com/index/chatgpt-memory-dreaming/ (June 4, 2026, "Dreaming: Better memory for a more helpful ChatGPT"). Verbatim: "The memories synthesized by dreaming are reviewable through a summary of them made visible in the memory summary page. From the memory summary, you can quickly glean the highlights of what ChatGPT knows about you, add or update information about yourself, and provide instructions on what topics ChatGPT should bring up and when. If you want to drill down into a particular area to learn more, just chat with the model." The post frames the old design's failure exactly as Adam does: saved memories "relied on strong cues", and "interacting with this system could feel like talking to someone who took a few notes, but still forgot everything that wasn't written down." Dreaming V0 shipped April 2025 as a supplement; V3 (June 2026) is the first version that is "standalone". Two hard numbers: a ~5x reduction in compute to serve dreaming, and "increase memory capacity for Plus and Pro users".
source: OpenAI blog, "Dreaming: Better memory for a more helpful ChatGPT", June 4 2026
applies_to_rekall: Direct validation of the one-document decision. Also note the ordering: OpenAI kept a per-item store underneath and made the document the *view*. Rekall could do the same — profile doc for injection/display, with the extractor still writing discrete patches.

claim: OpenAI's own help center draws the contrast between the two designs in one sentence, and names the summary the thing that "continually updates".
detail: help.openai.com/en/articles/8590148-memory-faq ("Memory in ChatGPT", page said "Updated: 2 days ago" when fetched 2026-09-21): "Improved Memory continually updates a broader summary of relevant context. Legacy saved memories use a more explicit list of individual memory items." Also: "The memory summary is a high-level view of information that ChatGPT may use to personalize responses. It does not necessarily include every detail or source that Memory can reference." And: "There is no separate storage limit for what ChatGPT can reference through chat history." Users can still switch back: Settings > Personalization > Memory > "Saved memories" (legacy) or "Try improved memory".
source: OpenAI Help Center, "Memory in ChatGPT", retrieved 2026-09-21
applies_to_rekall: Useful copy precedent for the settings screen. The "summary is a view, not the whole store" framing also gives Rekall an honest out if the doc is a condensation of underlying rows.

claim: On the ChatGPT memory summary, the user does NOT get a free-text editor over the document. They get four narrow affordances, three of which are corrections rather than edits.
detail: Verbatim list from the OpenAI help center: "Enter a correction in the text field." / "Highlight text and provide a correction." / "Select Don't mention this again when that option is available." / "Select Delete and turn off memory from the more options menu (•••)." Semantics are spelled out: "Don't mention this again reduces future references to the information. It does not delete the original source." "Delete and turn off memory deletes the remembered information shown in the summary and turns Memory off. It does not delete past chats." Separately, legacy saved-memory controls "can also include search, sorting, automatic prioritization, and version history."
source: OpenAI Help Center, "Memory in ChatGPT", retrieved 2026-09-21
applies_to_rekall: Strong argument against shipping a raw textarea. A "correct this" box plus highlight-to-correct keeps the doc machine-owned while giving the student agency, and each correction is a cheap incremental input to the next pass rather than a full rewrite.

claim: Claude went the opposite way on presentation: the user sees discrete, individually editable "Topics", not a document — even though what gets injected per turn is a small always-on profile plus a one-line index.
detail: support.claude.com/en/articles/11817273 ("Updated this week", retrieved 2026-09-21): "Claude saves memory as a set of individual topics as you chat, rather than summarizing conversations after they end." "Everything Claude remembers is listed under Topics. Select any topic to read it, then use the edit icon to change it or select 'Delete' to remove it. Fix something in one topic and the change applies to every conversation from then on." Legacy summary-based memory was migrated off, with an export window until September 9, 2026. Also: each Project gets "its own separate memory space and dedicated project summary."
source: Claude Help Center, "Use Claude's chat search and memory…", retrieved 2026-09-21; Anthropic blog Aug 25 2026
applies_to_rekall: The two frontier labs disagree on presentation, so this is a genuine product call, not a solved problem. Claude's answer suggests you can keep one injected document and still give per-section edit affordances by splitting the doc into named sections that are individually editable.

claim: Claude's actual injection budget is published in its leaked system prompt as a word count: the always-on profile document is capped at 300 words, and everything else is an index of one-line descriptions read on demand.
detail: From the Claude Fable 5.1 claude.ai system prompt (<memory_filesystem>, leaked ~Sept 1 2026): "/profile.md — who they are: name, role or title, where they work, what they work on at the level it stays stable, when they started. The test: would this line still be true in three months? … Keep it under 300 words." Per-turn injection is exactly three blocks: "the <profile>, <preferences> and <memory_listing> content is supplied to Claude on every turn". The listing is described as "each file's path, one-line summary, aliases, and sources" and explicitly "tells you which files exist, not what's in them"; full content requires memory_read(path). Earlier Opus 4.6 prompts instead injected one flat <userMemories> tag of comma-joined short facts ("User collects vintage typewriters, user's name is [name], user is looking to buy a new home in the Denver suburbs…").
source: asgeirtj/system_prompts_leaks + elder-plinius/CL4R1T4S, Claude Fable 5.1 (Sept 2026) and Claude Opus 4.6 raw (Feb 2026)
applies_to_rekall: 300 words is a defensible budget for an every-turn student profile — roughly 400 tokens, ~$0.0012/turn on Sonnet input. If Rekall's doc grows past that, the reference architecture is profile-always + everything-else-by-index, not a bigger blob.

claim: Claude's prompt gives the exact altitude rule Adam wants, in its memory_write tool description: save durable patterns, not specifics.
detail: memory_write tool description, verbatim: "Use this to save durable patterns you learn about the user — not today's specific events." The Calibration section elaborates with a horizon test: "would the line still be true and worth reading a month from now, in a conversation about something else? … The moving state of a task that finishes within a conversation or two — today's bug, this week's errand — fails it even when plainly stated: file the stable residue (the area exists, the decision, the constraint) and let the moving state expire with the task." And a phrasing rule: "Prefer durable phrasing over precise figures that go stale — 'meeting-heavy mornings' outlasts '10:00-10:15 team check-in', which breaks on the first calendar shift."
applies_to_rekall: Near drop-in prompt language for the extractor. "Confuses mitosis and meiosis phases" fails the month-from-now-in-a-different-conversation test; "jumps to the formula before reading the question" passes it. Adopt the horizon test verbatim as the filter.

claim: Claude's prompt also solves the "three specifics should become one pattern" problem with an explicit recurrence gate — a single mention is deliberately NOT filed, and the pattern is what gets filed when it recurs.
detail: Verbatim: "A single passing mention of a taste or pastime … is not yet memory material for this pass: file it when it recurs or when the user dwells on it, because a pattern is worth spotting once it is one." And a hard anti-generalization rule in the other direction: "one mention earns `[stated] mentioned X once`, not `[stated] X enthusiast`, and never upgrade a single mention into a generalization ('likes X' → 'likes the whole category X belongs to') — that's inference, not filing." The /topics/ folder is described as holding "once they recur or the user dwells on them, the patterns that started as passing mentions."
applies_to_rekall: This is the missing half of Adam's design. Precision is a symptom of writing on first sight. Requiring recurrence before anything is written naturally produces pattern-level observations — and it cuts write volume, which helps the token budget. Note Anthropic treats unsupported generalization as a *failure*, so the recurrence gate has to actually see the earlier evidence; a 12-message window may be too short, which argues for a small scratch "candidate signals" area separate from the profile.

claim: Anthropic explicitly forbids the cheap per-turn pass from consolidating, and triggers consolidation separately off a size signal. That is the direct answer to Adam's token constraint.
detail: Per-turn rule, verbatim: "In this background pass, edit an existing file only when the exchange changed what the file should say — a corrected fact, a superseded status, a genuinely new line. Never rewrite for phrasing, organization, tone, or completeness: an edit that leaves the file's meaning unchanged was not worth making, and consolidating or tidying files is never this pass's job." Consolidation is instead triggered by fullness: "reads report its size and free space, successful writes report the new size against the cap, and a note appears once a file is close to its cap. When that note appears, consolidate instead of shaving a few bytes to squeak under the cap: rewrite the file in a few larger edits that merge overlapping points and drop stale detail, or move a grown topic into its own file — and leave real headroom so the next few updates fit. Keep writing new facts as usual; fullness means reorganize, not stop writing."
source: Claude Fable 5.1 system prompt, <memory_filesystem> and the size-cap paragraph
applies_to_rekall: Two-tier design: every N turns, a cheap patch-only pass (append/replace one line, no rewrite); when the profile crosses ~80% of its word budget, a rarer consolidate pass that reads the whole doc and merges. The full rewrite Adam is worried about then happens maybe once every few dozen passes, not every pass.

claim: Both labs use a line-level string-replace op, not a rewrite, as the default write — and Anthropic's own tool description states the cost reason out loud.
detail: memory_str_replace description: "Cheaper than memory_write for small edits — you send only the text that changes, not the whole file." old_str must match "in exactly one place, including whitespace and newlines — zero or multiple matches are rejected". Writes carry a 12-character `if_version` optimistic-concurrency token from the last read; "A version conflict or a failed match returns the current content so you can retry in one turn." memory_append exists for genuinely new lines but is discouraged: "files are size-capped, so prefer editing and condensing over repeated appends." The public developer-facing memory tool (platform.claude.com, tool type `memory_20250818`) exposes the same six commands: view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, rename.
source: Claude Fable 5.1 tool schemas; platform.claude.com memory tool docs
applies_to_rekall: The incremental mechanism Adam needs, with a caveat worth budgeting for: exact-match str_replace fails often on model-generated old_str. The published mitigation is to return the file's current content inside the error so the model self-corrects in the same pass, rather than failing the write.

claim: ChatGPT's dreamed profile is injected as several separate labelled sections, each note carrying an explicit Confidence field — and one of those sections is literally about response preferences rather than facts.
detail: From the leaked GPT-5 system prompt (dated Aug 23 2025 in-file), the injected blocks in order are: `# User Bio` (a templated profile: Preferred name / Role / Other Information), `# User's Instructions`, `# Model Set Context` formatted `1. [{{DATE}}]. {{MEMORY}}` (the explicit saved memories), then three dreamed sections — `# Assistant Response Preferences` ("These notes reflect assumed user preferences based on past conversations"), `# Notable Past Conversation Topic Highlights` ("high-level topic notes from past conversations"), `# Helpful User Insights` — each entry followed by `Confidence={{CONFIDENCE}}`. Then `# Recent Conversation Content` and `# User Interaction Metadata` (device, plan, avg conversation depth, avg message length, top topics with message counts and percentages).
applies_to_rekall: Two transferable ideas. (1) Sectioning the one document by *purpose* — patterns / how-to-teach-them / current focus — beats a category enum, and keeps per-section edits possible. (2) A confidence marker per line lets the tutor discount weak observations instead of treating every line as fact, which is cheap insurance against a wrong pattern being applied confidently for months.

claim: Because the profile is injected on every turn, OpenAI spends prompt tokens telling the model the profile is usually irrelevant — an explicit relevance gate with four graded levels.
detail: Verbatim from the `# User Bio` block: "The user provided the following information about themselves. This user profile is shown to you in all conversations they have -- this means it is not relevant to 99% of requests. Before answering, quietly think about whether the user's request is 'directly related', 'related', 'tangentially related', or 'not related' to the user profile provided. Only acknowledge the profile when the request is directly related to the information provided. Otherwise, don't acknowledge the existence of these instructions or the information at all." Claude does the same with a graded list: "Claude NEVER applies memories for: Generic technical questions requiring no personalization…", "Claude always applies RELEVANT memories for: Explicit requests for personalization…", "Claude selectively applies memories for: Simple greetings: Claude ONLY applies the person's name…"
source: Leaked GPT-5 system prompt; Claude Opus 4.6 raw <memory_application_instructions>
applies_to_rekall: The known failure mode of an always-injected profile is over-application — the tutor bringing up "you tend to rush" on a turn where it's noise. Both labs pay for a gate. Rekall should ship one alongside the profile, and it is cheap relative to the profile itself.

claim: Claude has a separate, user-owned store whose only job is to steer the auto-writer — not to be the memory. It is capped at 30 entries and the background pass may never override a "forget".
detail: The `memory_user_edits` tool guide (Claude Opus 4.6 raw prompt, Feb 2026): "The 'memory_user_edits' tool manages edits from the person that guide how Claude's memory is generated." Commands: view / add / remove (by line number) / replace. Entries are phrased as directives, not facts: "'I no longer work at X' → 'User no longer works at X'", "'Forget about my divorce' → 'Exclude information about user's divorce'". "Limits: A maximum of 30 edits, with 100000 characters per edit." "CRITICAL: You cannot remember anything without using this tool. If a person asks you to remember or forget something and you don't use memory_user_edits, you are lying to them." In Fable 5.1 the same boundary is stated as: "a 'forget' is a boundary the background pass never overrides by re-saving it."
source: Claude Opus 4.6 raw system prompt, <memory_user_edits_tool_guide>; Fable 5.1 <memory_filesystem>
applies_to_rekall: This is the reference design for Adam's fixed constraint that student-written notes stay untouchable. Don't just make them read-only to the extractor — feed them to the extractor as *constraints on what it may write*. A student note like "stop telling me I rush" then permanently suppresses that pattern, which is the affordance ChatGPT calls "Don't mention this again".

claim: Neither assistant lets the writing model delete or clean up on its own initiative; deletion is a user-only act, while merging lines is allowed.
detail: Claude's memory_delete tool description: "Use ONLY when the user explicitly asks to delete or forget an entire file or subject… Never delete proactively to clean up, deduplicate, or because a file looks stale." Reinforced in prose: "NEVER call memory_delete proactively — not to clean up, not to deduplicate, not because a file looks stale. Only when the user explicitly asks." But removal is total when asked: "delete the line entirely — don't soften it ('used to like X', 'X but not anymore')… Also remove anything you derived solely from the removed fact." ChatGPT side: "Deleting a chat alone does not necessarily delete a separate saved memory", and OpenAI "may retain logs of deleted saved memories for up to 30 days for safety and debugging purposes."
source: Claude Fable 5.1 tool schemas + prose; OpenAI Help Center memory FAQ
applies_to_rekall: Draw the line at subject-level deletion vs line-level merging. Consolidation (three specifics → one pattern) is a merge and should be allowed; dropping a whole area of the student's profile should require the student. Also: when the student deletes a pattern, drop anything the extractor derived from it.

claim: Both products deliberately suppress "Memory updated" chatter from the model and let the UI carry it; the visible surface is a chip or an inline notice, not a sentence in the reply.
detail: Claude Fable 5.1: "Never announce saves. The background pass runs after your reply, so you can't see or report what it files; and for the writes you make yourself on an explicit request, the UI already shows a 'Saved memory' chip, so narrating them just duplicates it." Sensitive-topic writes get a dedicated surface: "Each time Claude saves something on one of these topics, a notice appears above the message box so you can review it or update your settings." ChatGPT's current equivalent is per-response provenance rather than a save toast: "When ChatGPT uses relevant personal context, Sources may appear below the response", and per source the user may "correct or delete a saved memory", "delete a referenced chat", or "mark a source as relevant or not relevant".
source: Claude Fable 5.1 system prompt; Claude Help Center; OpenAI Help Center memory FAQ
applies_to_rekall: For a background pass that runs every N turns, a chip is the wrong unit — the tutor can't see what was written. Better: a subtle "profile updated" affordance on the turn boundary that opens a diff, plus ChatGPT-style provenance when the tutor actually leans on a pattern ("this is why I asked you to read the question aloud"). Also, an explicit no-narrating rule in the tutor prompt.

claim: The written-vs-declined boundary in ChatGPT's bio tool is four named anti-patterns plus a category blocklist, and an explicit user-override escape hatch.
detail: Verbatim: "Don't store random, trivial, or overly personal facts. In particular, avoid: Overly-personal details that could feel creepy. Short-lived facts that won't matter soon. Random details that lack clear future relevance. Redundant information that we already know about the user." Trigger side: "The user has shared information that will be useful in future conversations and valid for a long time… User information is worth saving in memory if it is likely to change your future responses in similar situations." Plus an asymmetry worth copying: an explicit user request always wins — "you should always call the bio tool, even if the requested information has already been stored, appears extremely trivial or fleeting" and "The exception to all of the above instructions … is if the user explicitly requests that you save or forget information."
applies_to_rekall: "Worth saving if it is likely to change your future responses in similar situations" is a sharper test than a category enum, and it is the one that kills "confuses mitosis and meiosis" (changes one future response) while keeping "jumps to the formula" (changes how every problem is introduced). Keep the student-override asymmetry: if a student asks the tutor to remember something, write it regardless of the altitude bar.

claim: Claude's already-filed rule is a soft instruction to the writer, not a hard rejection at the storage layer — the opposite of Rekall's 60% containment reject.
detail: Verbatim: "Already filed means already remembered. A fact that restates, rephrases, or is implied by a line in the listing, <profile>, or <preferences> is not new material: don't re-file it under another path, and don't edit a file just to restate what it already says in different words. New material is what changes the store — a fact it lacks, a correction, a supersession. If everything that meets the bar is already filed, there is nothing to save." Critically, the model sees the existing content before writing ("For any file in <memory_listing>, memory_read it first and then update instead of overwriting"), so a generalization arrives as a str_replace over the three specifics, which the store has no reason to reject.
applies_to_rekall: Names the root cause precisely. Dedupe belongs in the prompt with the current profile in view, not in a similarity check at insert time. Once the extractor can read and patch, "generalize three specifics into one pattern" is a supersession — the category the rule explicitly welcomes — and the 60% overlap that currently triggers rejection becomes the signal that a merge is warranted.

claim: Gemini is the cautionary end of the spectrum: no viewable memory artifact at all, no per-item edit, and Google's own help page tells you to interrogate the model to find out what it used.
detail: support.google.com/gemini/answer/16598469 (retrieved 2026-09-21): memory lives behind Settings & help > Personal Intelligence > Memory (a single on/off toggle). "To check if Gemini used your past chats, just ask Gemini, 'Did you use any info from past chats?'" To delete: "To delete something that Gemini remembered about you, delete all chats with this info from Gemini Apps Activity." To correct: "Correct Gemini directly in your chat" — followed by the hedge "While Gemini continues to improve, it might not always get it right." Requires 18+, a personal account, and Keep Activity on; default activity retention is 18 months (options 3 / 36 months / off). "Saved info" is a separate, manually curated list with its own toggle.
source: Google Gemini Apps Help, "Get personalization with memory of your past Gemini chats" + "Get personalization in Gemini Apps", retrieved 2026-09-21
applies_to_rekall: Gemini's split — auto "Personal context" (invisible, source-deletion only) vs manual "Saved info" (a visible list) — is the same separation Adam already fixed between auto profile and student notes. But note which half Google made inspectable: the manual one. If Rekall's auto profile is the *more* consequential half, making it the visible one is a differentiator, not just parity.

claim: The open-source reference implementation for "one document, incrementally patched, with a background consolidator" is Letta's memory blocks plus sleep-time agents, and it publishes both the character limit and the consolidation op.
detail: Letta memory blocks are "structured sections of the agent's context window that persist across all interactions. They are always visible - no retrieval needed", rendered as XML: <memory_blocks><persona><description>…</description><metadata>…</metadata><value>…</value></persona><human>…</human></memory_blocks>, where metadata reports current chars against the limit. Default block limit is 2,000 characters (configurable; docs examples use 5000). Edit ops are memory_insert / memory_replace / memory_rethink / memory_finish_edits; memory_replace is exact string match, and "if the old_value doesn't exist exactly as stored in memory (including whitespace, punctuation, newlines), the replacement silently fails". memory_rethink is the consolidation primitive: re-evaluate a block, integrate new and updated facts, replace outdated information, avoid redundancy. Sleep-time compute (Letta, arXiv 2504.13171, April 2025) runs those agents between conversations to "consolidate fragmented memories into coherent entries, identify patterns across conversations, and reorganize and deduplicate memory blocks".
source: docs.letta.com (memory blocks, core memory), letta.com/blog/sleep-time-compute, arXiv 2504.13171
applies_to_rekall: 2,000 characters (~500 tokens) is the community default for an always-injected profile block, consistent with Claude's 300 words. The in-block metadata showing chars-used/limit is a cheap trick worth copying: it lets the extractor decide for itself whether this pass should append or consolidate, without Rekall needing a separate trigger.

claim: Microsoft Copilot is the third datapoint and stays on discrete items with per-item delete — so the summary-document design is currently a minority of two-and-a-half, not an industry consensus.
detail: Copilot Memory (Microsoft Support / Microsoft Learn, "Manage Copilot Memory in Microsoft 365 Copilot"): memories are managed from Chat settings > Personalization > Saved memories > "Manage saved memories"; users "can view, edit, or delete your memories anytime from the Settings pane", with Delete next to each memory and a "Delete all memories" button. Discovery is conversational — ask Copilot "What do you know about me?" Write/forget is instruction-driven ("Remember that I'm vegetarian", "Forget my ex's birthday"). Turning the Saved memories toggle off "doesn't automatically delete already saved memories".
source: Microsoft Support / Microsoft Learn Copilot personalization and memory pages
applies_to_rekall: Background only, with one lift: "What do you know about me?" as a first-class conversational entry point. In a tutor, "what have you noticed about how I study?" is a natural way to expose the profile without a settings screen, and it doubles as the drill-down OpenAI points to ("just chat with the model").
